section: A question with a small answer and a large one
objective: Identify the three scales used to examine technology-related change
stem: Which three scales organise Chapter 1’s examination of what technology changes?

options.text: Hardware, software and networks.
options.rationale: These are technical resources, not the three scales at which the chapter examines change.

options.text: Organisation, industry and society.
options.rationale: The chapter examines how a firm works, how industry boundaries change and how consequences reach society.

options.text: People, processes and data.
options.rationale: These are parts of an information system, not the scales of change.

options.text: Revenue, cost and profit.
options.rationale: These are financial measures; the chapter’s scales extend beyond financial performance.

section: One company, twice
objective: Explain why a customer-unfriendly rule may persist
stem: A rental business earns substantial revenue from overdue charges. Customers dislike them, and a manager proposes removing them. What issue must the proposal address?

options.text: How to teach customers to appreciate the existing charge.
options.rationale: Explaining a charge does not address how the business will operate financially after removing it.

options.text: How quickly the software can stop calculating the charge.
options.rationale: Changing the calculation is only one part; removing the charge also changes revenue.

options.text: How the replacement arrangement will serve customers and remain affordable.
options.rationale: The fee supports revenue even while irritating customers; a replacement must work operationally and financially.

options.text: How to demonstrate that every competitor has removed the charge.
options.rationale: Competitor choices do not establish whether this firm can afford and operate its replacement.

section: One company, twice
objective: Distinguish removing a rule from automating its administration
stem: A tool-hire shop wants to remove work caused by overdue charges. Which proposal changes the rule that creates that work?

options.text: Offer a flat subscription with no due date for each tool held.
options.rationale: Removing the due date removes the reason to calculate overdue charges, though tool tracking is still needed.

options.text: Send overdue-charge notices automatically each evening.
options.rationale: This automates notice delivery while retaining the rule and its associated charges.

options.text: Let customers pay overdue charges through a mobile app.
options.rationale: An easier payment channel does not remove the underlying overdue-charge rule.

options.text: Give staff a faster screen for reviewing overdue charges.
options.rationale: A faster screen improves administration of the existing rule rather than removing it.

section: One company, twice
objective: Identify work that remains after a business rule is removed
stem: A subscription library removes return deadlines. Its manager also proposes deleting records of which customer holds each item because late fees are gone. What is the flaw?

options.text: A subscription cannot generate revenue without late fees.
options.rationale: A subscription payment can generate revenue; late fees are not a necessary part of that model.

options.text: The library must retain deadlines to keep using software.
options.rationale: Software can support different business rules; deadlines are not a technical requirement.

options.text: Removing deadlines eliminates the need to receive returns.
options.rationale: Items still need to be returned and made available to others.

options.text: Customer-item records still support returns and future fulfilment.
options.rationale: The fee-related task disappears, but organising circulation still requires accurate records.

section: One company, twice
objective: Identify a managerial responsibility during a delivery-model transition
stem: A training company adds streamed courses while customers still use its mailed learning kits. Which decision most closely matches the Netflix transition discussed in the chapter?

options.text: Which streaming supplier offers the newest features?
options.rationale: Features matter, but they do not settle how to support the old service while building the new one.

options.text: What to build, what to maintain and when to retire the kit service.
options.rationale: The transition requires choices about new capability and continuing responsibilities to existing customers.

options.text: How to remove the kit service from next month’s sales report.
options.rationale: Changing a report does not remove obligations to customers still using that service.

options.text: How to persuade all customers that streaming is technically superior.
options.rationale: Persuasion does not establish readiness or provide a workable transition for existing users.

section: One industry, then another
objective: Recognise a change in an industry boundary
stem: A retailer develops delivery-coordination services and begins selling them to unrelated manufacturers. Those manufacturers now compare it with logistics suppliers. Which change is most directly illustrated?

options.text: A change in the retailer’s internal staff reporting lines.
options.rationale: The scenario concerns a new market relationship, not who reports to whom inside the retailer.

options.text: A change in society’s rules for public debate.
options.rationale: No change in public debate is described.

options.text: A change confined to how the retailer displays its catalogue.
options.rationale: Selling coordination to other firms goes beyond changing the retail catalogue.

options.text: A change in the boundary between retail and logistics services.
options.rationale: A capability developed in one business now serves customers in another market.

section: One industry, then another
objective: Reject the assumption that success transfers automatically across industries
stem: A successful online retailer proposes entering home care. Its director says, “Our retail success proves we can make this work.” Which response follows Chapter 1’s treatment of Haven?

options.text: Require the new service to use exactly the same operating model as retail.
options.rationale: A new industry brings different practical requirements; copying the old model is not proof of fitness.

options.text: Assume the new venture will fail because it lies outside retail.
options.rationale: Haven’s closure does not prove that every move into a new industry must fail.

options.text: Examine the new industry’s needs, economics and operating difficulties.
options.rationale: Previous success can provide capabilities, but the new setting still needs its own assessment.

options.text: Accept the claim if the retailer has a larger technology budget than rivals.
options.rationale: A larger budget does not establish that the service will meet the new industry’s requirements.

section: One society
objective: Recognise a societal question that extends beyond company performance
stem: A profitable neighbourhood platform changes which posts residents see. Which question examines the societal scale most directly?

options.text: Whose views become visible, who bears harm and who can challenge the rules?
options.rationale: These questions concern consequences and participation beyond the platform’s own financial results.

options.text: Which subscription price would maximise the platform’s revenue?
options.rationale: This primarily examines the firm’s revenue rather than its wider social consequences.

options.text: Which staffing schedule would reduce the support team’s overtime?
options.rationale: This concerns the organisation of work within the firm.

options.text: Which server upgrade would reduce the platform’s monthly operating cost?
options.rationale: This focuses on an internal technical and cost decision.

section: One society
objective: Distinguish evidence of tool use from evidence of causation
stem: Participants in a community campaign report using a social platform to organise meetings. A consultant concludes that the platform caused the campaign’s success. What does the reported evidence establish?

options.text: The platform was sufficient to make the campaign succeed.
options.rationale: Evidence of use does not show that the tool alone was sufficient for success.

options.text: The campaign would have failed without the platform.
options.rationale: The account does not establish what would have happened without it.

options.text: People used the platform to coordinate; its causal contribution needs more evidence.
options.rationale: The account supports use of the tool, not the stronger claim that it caused the outcome.

options.text: The platform’s design had no effect because people made the decisions.
options.rationale: Human choices and technical capability can both matter; the evidence does not establish no effect.

section: What you just watched
objective: Explain why different scales require different evidence
stem: A platform’s revenue rises while residents report harmful effects from its recommendation rules. Its manager says the revenue increase proves the platform benefits society. What is the strongest criticism?

options.text: Higher revenue proves that the residents’ reports are inaccurate.
options.rationale: Financial performance cannot establish whether those reports are true or false.

options.text: Evidence of company performance does not settle the distribution of social benefits and costs.
options.rationale: The manager uses evidence at one scale to answer a different question about wider consequences.

options.text: Reports of social harm prove the company will become unprofitable.
options.rationale: Social effects do not by themselves determine the firm’s financial survival.

options.text: Financial and social questions must concern entirely different companies.
options.rationale: The scales overlap; the same company can raise both kinds of question.

section: What you just watched
objective: Distinguish information technology from an information system
stem: Which statement best expresses Chapter 1’s distinction between IT and an information system?

options.text: IT includes staff and procedures; an information system includes only the records.
options.rationale: This reverses and narrows the distinction; records are only one part of the whole system.

options.text: IT concerns daily work; an information system is used only for strategic decisions.
options.rationale: Information systems support both activities and decisions, including ordinary service work.

options.text: IT and information system are interchangeable names for equipment and software.
options.rationale: Equipment and software are the technology component, not the whole information system.

options.text: IT is equipment and software within a system of people, processes, data and technology.
options.rationale: The whole system includes the arrangements through which people use records and technology.

section: What you just watched
objective: Diagnose a service failure beyond functioning equipment
stem: A parcel is recorded against the wrong customer account. The computers and network work normally, but the correct customer’s next order is blocked. What should the manager arrange?

options.text: Give a responsible employee access, a checking procedure and authority to correct the record.
options.rationale: The service needs accurate data and a workable route for a person to establish and correct the error.

options.text: Replace the network because a working network would prevent account errors.
options.rationale: A functioning network can transmit an incorrectly entered or assigned record.

options.text: Wait for the next equipment upgrade before investigating the customer’s problem.
options.rationale: The error already needs attention; an upgrade does not establish or correct what happened.

options.text: Ask the customer to reorder while retaining the existing account record.
options.rationale: Reordering does not resolve the incorrect record that blocked service.

section: What you just watched
objective: Identify the data component in a business service
stem: A bicycle-repair shop uses an app to manage bookings. Which item is data within that information system?

options.text: The mechanic assigned to handle customer enquiries.
options.rationale: The mechanic is part of the people component.

options.text: The recorded bicycle number, requested repair and promised collection time.
options.rationale: These recorded facts describe the work and commitments on which service depends.

options.text: The steps for checking in, repairing and returning a bicycle.
options.rationale: The connected steps make up the process.

options.text: The tablet and booking software used at the counter.
options.rationale: The equipment and software are the technology component.

section: What you just watched
objective: Identify a missing organisational condition for correcting errors
stem: A shop’s software lets staff see and edit stock records. A known error keeps blocking sales because nobody knows who may approve a correction. What is the most direct missing element?

options.text: A larger database to hold additional stock records.
options.rationale: Storage capacity does not resolve who may approve a correction.

options.text: An extra screen showing the same incorrect stock figure.
options.rationale: Making the error more visible does not establish authority to fix it.

options.text: An agreed responsibility and approval route for correcting stock records.
options.rationale: The technical capability exists, but the organisation has not established who can use it to resolve the problem.

options.text: A requirement to record every blocked sale before considering corrections.
options.rationale: Recording failures may reveal their scale, but it does not resolve the missing authority.

section: Improvement is not the same as advantage
objective: Distinguish value creation from value capture
stem: Which question is primarily about value capture?

options.text: Who keeps the benefit produced by the change?
options.rationale: Value capture concerns how benefits are retained or distributed among parties.

options.text: Are the benefits worth more than the resources consumed?
options.rationale: This is the chapter’s value-creation question.

options.text: Which equipment and software support the work?
options.rationale: This identifies technology rather than who keeps the benefit.

options.text: Which steps turn a request into a delivered service?
options.rationale: This identifies a process rather than the distribution of benefits.

section: Improvement is not the same as advantage
objective: Distinguish a useful improvement from a sustainable advantage
stem: Two competing laundry services introduce equally convenient booking apps at similar cost. Both reduce customer effort. What can a manager reasonably conclude?

options.text: The first service to launch must retain a lasting advantage.
options.rationale: Arriving early can help, but it does not establish that rivals cannot copy or overcome the benefit.

options.text: Neither app creates value because both services have one.
options.rationale: Customers can benefit from an improvement even when competitors offer it too.

options.text: Each service has a sustainable advantage because its customers benefit.
options.rationale: Customer benefit does not establish an edge that rivals cannot readily reproduce.

options.text: Both may create value, but the apps alone do not establish a lasting competitive edge.
options.rationale: A useful improvement and sustainable competitive advantage are separate claims.

section: Improvement is not the same as advantage
objective: Identify how a supplier can capture a business’s savings
stem: Assume a delivery tool produces $600 in monthly operating savings for a shop, with no other costs or benefits apart from its $550 monthly fee. How much of those savings does the shop retain after paying the supplier?

options.text: $600, because the operating savings are the value captured by the shop.
options.rationale: This ignores the fee paid to the supplier from those savings.

options.text: $50, because the supplier’s fee absorbs $550 of the savings.
options.rationale: The shop retains $600 minus $550; the split illustrates why savings and retained benefit differ.

options.text: $550, because the fee measures the shop’s retained benefit.
options.rationale: The fee is paid out to the supplier, not retained by the shop.

options.text: $1,150, because savings and supplier revenue are both benefits to the shop.
options.rationale: Adding the fee treats an outgoing payment as an additional benefit to the shop.

section: Improvement is not the same as advantage
objective: Evaluate first-mover advantage using evidence about rivals
stem: A repair chain launched online booking first. Rivals now offer similar convenience at similar cost. Which additional finding would best support a continuing edge for the first chain?

options.text: Its booking page still carries the earliest launch date.
options.rationale: Being first is historical evidence, not evidence that the benefit remains difficult to overcome.

options.text: Its managers refer to the service as a digital transformation.
options.rationale: The label does not establish a difference in customer preference or cost.

options.text: Customers prefer its reliable service, supported by arrangements rivals struggle to reproduce.
options.rationale: A preferred offering with hard-to-copy supporting arrangements can provide a continuing competitive edge.

options.text: Its app uses the same readily available software as the competitors.
options.rationale: Shared accessible software does not explain why this chain should outperform its rivals.

section: Try the question on a smaller business
objective: Identify why faster order entry may not shorten the total wait
stem: A café introduces instant mobile ordering, but drink preparation is already the slowest step. Staffing and equipment stay the same. What risk should the owner examine?

options.text: More accepted orders may lengthen the wait for preparation.
options.rationale: Faster order entry can increase work arriving at a step whose capacity has not changed.

options.text: Instant ordering will increase preparation capacity by the same proportion.
options.rationale: Taking an order faster does not make staff prepare drinks faster.

options.text: The visible counter queue will measure the whole customer wait.
options.rationale: Customers may now wait in a digital queue that is not visible at the counter.

options.text: Preparation time will stop mattering once customers have paid remotely.
options.rationale: Remote payment does not remove the customer’s need to receive the drink.

section: Try the question on a smaller business
objective: Connect a service promise to capacity and control
stem: A café wants its app to offer dependable collection times. Which arrangement best supports that promise?

options.text: Let customers choose any time and ask staff to sort orders when they arrive.
options.rationale: Unrestricted promises can exceed preparation capacity before staff can respond.

options.text: Use last term’s average demand to offer the same slots every day.
options.rationale: A fixed historical average does not keep current availability aligned with actual capacity.

options.text: Accept all orders and explain delays only when customers reach the counter.
options.rationale: This responds after making promises the café may be unable to meet.

options.text: Offer feasible slots, update availability and give staff authority to pause new orders.
options.rationale: The promise is supported by capacity, current data and a person who can act when the café falls behind.

section: Try the question on a smaller business
objective: Identify decision authority needed during a service disruption
stem: The café owner alone can approve refunds but is unreachable during lunch. The app correctly identifies a late order. What should the owner settle before expanding the service?

options.text: Whether the app can display the late-order message in a larger font.
options.rationale: Visibility does not give staff authority to provide a remedy.

options.text: Who may inform the customer and authorise a remedy during service.
options.rationale: The service needs an available person with agreed responsibility and authority when a promise fails.

options.text: Whether late orders should disappear from the app after collection.
options.rationale: Removing a record does not resolve the response needed when the order is late.

options.text: Whether customers can be required to contact the owner after lunch.
options.rationale: Deferring every case preserves the availability problem rather than providing a workable service response.

section: Try the question on a smaller business
objective: Choose evidence that evaluates a proposed service improvement fairly
stem: A café’s app receives 300 downloads. The owner wants to expand because the app was intended to improve service. Which evidence would best support that decision?

options.text: Download growth compared with the previous week’s advertising spending.
options.rationale: Adoption and advertising do not show whether waiting times, errors and service costs improved.

options.text: The vendor’s average customer rating across cafés of all sizes.
options.rationale: Other users’ ratings do not establish what happened in this café under comparable conditions.

options.text: Waiting times and order errors across similar periods, with app charges and staff time included.
options.rationale: This tests the intended outcome against a relevant comparison while accounting for the resources consumed.

options.text: Time spent entering app orders, excluding preparation and correction work.
options.rationale: A faster single step may hide delays and costs elsewhere in the service.

section: Your turn
objective: Label an unverified explanation as an assumption
stem: A student notices that a gym charges a cancellation fee. Without asking anyone or checking records, the student writes, “The fee pays for unused staff time.” How should this statement be presented?

options.text: As an assumption about the fee’s purpose that still needs evidence.
options.rationale: The explanation may be plausible, but the student has not established why the gym charges the fee.

options.text: As a verified fact because unused staff time is a possible cost.
options.rationale: A possible business reason is not evidence that it is this gym’s reason.

options.text: As proof that removing the fee would necessarily cause a loss.
options.rationale: Neither the purpose nor the financial effect of removal has been established.

options.text: As evidence that the gym’s customers benefit from the fee.
options.rationale: The statement concerns a possible organisational purpose, not evidence of customer benefit.

section: Your turn
objective: Recognise a technology prediction with a mechanism and a limitation
stem: Which forecast best follows the chapter’s closing guidance for explaining what a new capability might change?

options.text: “This tool attracts the most headlines, so firms using it will outperform their rivals.”
options.rationale: Attention does not establish the mechanism of improvement or a reason the prediction might fail.

options.text: “This tool will remove delays because faster software always produces faster service.”
options.rationale: The claim ignores the rest of the process and assumes the outcome instead of explaining it.

options.text: “This tool helped a large retailer, so its success will carry over to every small shop.”
options.rationale: An outcome in one setting does not establish success in another with different conditions.

options.text: “Shared stock updates could let branches fulfil one another’s orders, unless records are too inaccurate to rely on.”
options.rationale: The forecast links a capability to a changed arrangement and identifies a condition that could prevent success.

section: A fence falls down
objective: Recognise why internal compliance does not establish a satisfactory customer result
stem: In the fence teaching case, the insurer applied the policy correctly and met its internal deadlines, but the customer wanted to leave. What should a manager investigate next?

options.text: Whether meeting the deadlines should close the service review.
options.rationale: Internal deadlines do not establish that the customer received timely explanations or experienced a workable process.

options.text: Whether dissatisfaction requires increasing the payment above the policy amount.
options.rationale: The problem may concern effort, uncertainty or explanation; dissatisfaction alone does not establish that the settlement should change.

options.text: What the customer understood, waited for and had to do across the whole claim.
options.rationale: The gap concerns the complete experience, which departmental compliance measures may miss.

options.text: Whether each department can provide another copy of its compliance report.
options.rationale: More evidence of the same internal measures may leave the customer’s experience unexplained.

section: The question underneath the technology
objective: State the distinction made by the Hammer test
stem: What distinction does the Hammer test ask a manager to make?

options.text: Whether a proposal makes an existing step faster or removes the reason it exists.
options.rationale: The test separates automating existing work from changing the arrangement that creates it.

options.text: Whether a proposal uses newer software or retains the current software.
options.rationale: Software age does not determine whether work has been redesigned.

options.text: Whether a proposal reduces staff numbers or keeps staffing unchanged.
options.rationale: Headcount alone does not show what work is necessary or why it exists.

options.text: Whether a proposal benefits customers or benefits the organisation.
options.rationale: The test concerns the reason for work; a change can benefit both parties.

section: The question underneath the technology
objective: Identify the supporting changes needed to remove a document safely
stem: A wholesaler proposes paying suppliers from purchase orders and receipt records instead of waiting for invoices. Receiving staff currently enter incomplete records several days after delivery. What must the redesign address?

options.text: Keep receipt entry unchanged and treat every ordered item as delivered.
options.rationale: An order records what was requested, not what actually arrived; this could authorise unsupported payments.

options.text: Move the invoice queue to finance while describing it as invoice-free processing.
options.rationale: The work and its dependence on invoices remain; changing the queue’s location does not remove them.

options.text: Scan incoming invoices more quickly and retain the existing payment rules.
options.rationale: This may improve the current process, but it does not make receipt-based payment workable.

options.text: Establish timely, accurate receipt recording and rules that authorise payment from those records.
options.rationale: Removing the invoice depends on changing the information and responsibilities that make payment reliable.

section: Start with what the customer experienced
objective: Identify an inference hidden in a customer chronology
stem: A customer reports, “I submitted a repair request Monday, received an email Tuesday and collected the repaired item Friday.” Which addition to the analyst’s map is an inference rather than something stated in the account?

options.text: The customer submitted the request on Monday.
options.rationale: This event is directly stated in the customer’s account.

options.text: A separate correspondence team prepared Tuesday’s email.
options.rationale: The email’s arrival does not establish which person, team or system produced it.

options.text: The customer received an email on Tuesday.
options.rationale: The account explicitly reports receiving the email that day.

options.text: The customer collected the repaired item on Friday.
options.rationale: Collection and its date are directly reported.

section: Start with what the customer experienced
objective: Choose a verification question that distinguishes capability from assignment of responsibility
stem: An employee had to email a receipt to finance after submitting an expense form. The analyst concludes, “The expense system cannot accept attachments.” Which question best tests that explanation?

options.text: How many employees dislike emailing receipts?
options.rationale: This could measure burden, but it does not establish whether attachments are technically possible or why email was used.

options.text: Which vendor offers the cheapest attachment feature?
options.rationale: Selecting a replacement feature assumes the capability is missing before verifying that assumption.

options.text: How quickly did finance reply to the employee’s email?
options.rationale: Response time does not establish the system’s capability or the rule governing receipt submission.

options.text: Can the system accept receipts, and what rule or circumstance led this employee to use email?
options.rationale: The system may have the capability while a rule, configuration or particular case explains the email route.

section: Build a map that can be challenged
objective: Choose process boundaries that match the outcome being examined
stem: A repair shop wants to understand the customer’s wait from reporting a fault until receiving the repaired item and an explanation. Which map boundaries fit that question?

options.text: Start at the fault report; end at customer receipt of the item and explanation.
options.rationale: These boundaries include the complete interval and outcome the shop wants to examine.

options.text: Start when a technician begins work; end when the repair is completed.
options.rationale: This excludes intake, queuing and return to the customer.

options.text: Start when the parts order is placed; end when parts arrive.
options.rationale: This maps one supporting activity, not the customer’s complete wait.

options.text: Start when the repair is invoiced; end when the customer pays.
options.rationale: This examines billing and payment rather than the requested service experience.

section: Build a map that can be challenged
objective: Represent an unsupported exception branch as an uncertainty to verify
stem: A registration analyst maps what happens when a class is full. Staff disagree about whether the request goes to a waiting list or directly to an adviser, and no cases have been checked. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Choose the waiting-list route because it appears in the policy manual.
options.rationale: The manual is evidence of intended procedure, but it does not settle how the disputed process actually runs.

options.text: Draw both routes as confirmed alternatives without conditions.
options.rationale: This turns unresolved accounts into established process facts and leaves their selection unexplained.

options.text: Mark the route as unresolved and check recent cases and responsible staff before confirming branches.
options.rationale: A map should expose uncertainty and use evidence to establish when each path is followed.

options.text: Omit full-class requests so the main process remains simple.
options.rationale: Removing a relevant exception hides work that may require different evidence or authority.

section: Build a map that can be challenged
objective: Select evidence that discriminates among explanations for a delay
stem: A log shows a repair waited four days after inspection. A supervisor attributes the wait to insufficient technicians. Which check would best test that diagnosis?

options.text: Compare the total employee count with that of a larger repair firm.
options.rationale: A staffing comparison does not show whether this repair was ready for a technician or waiting for something else.

options.text: Trace the repair’s queue, missing-information requests and staff workload during those four days.
options.rationale: These records can distinguish insufficient capacity from missing information or incorrect routing.

options.text: Ask customers whether four days feels too long.
options.rationale: Customer views help assess the experience but do not establish the cause of this delay.

options.text: Estimate the cost of hiring a technician before examining the file.
options.rationale: A cost estimate evaluates a proposed remedy without establishing that staffing caused the wait.

section: Build a map that can be challenged
objective: Reconcile conflicting staff accounts and records before confirming a map
stem: A reimbursement manager says approval happens on the day of submission. Several system records show approval two days later. What should an analyst do before finalising the as-is map?

options.text: Use the manager’s account alone because staff understand why the work happens.
options.rationale: Staff can explain work, but their general account does not settle the timing shown in particular cases.

options.text: Walk through the sampled cases with the manager and establish what the timestamps record.
options.rationale: Staff explanations and records can be checked together to distinguish actual waiting from differences in how events are recorded.

options.text: Use the timestamps alone to conclude the manager deliberately described the process falsely.
options.rationale: The discrepancy does not establish intent; the records may represent a different event or omit context.

options.text: Put one day on the map as a compromise between the two accounts.
options.rationale: Averaging conflicting descriptions creates an unsupported timeline rather than resolving what happened.

section: Diagnose the failure before changing the process
objective: Distinguish an explanation failure from a pure speed problem
stem: Employees expect full reimbursement for hotel stays but learn about a nightly limit only after submitting expenses. Finance cuts processing from ten days to six, yet disputes continue. Which explanation best fits these facts?

options.text: Six days must still exceed the legal processing deadline.
options.rationale: No legal deadline is supplied; the facts do not support that explanation.

options.text: The nightly limit must be removed because a faster process failed.
options.rationale: The evidence does not establish that the limit is unnecessary; it points to when employees learn about it.

options.text: The payment calculation must be incorrect whenever employees dispute it.
options.rationale: A correctly calculated amount can still conflict with an expectation formed without the relevant rule.

options.text: Faster processing leaves the late communication of the limit unresolved.
options.rationale: Speed alone does not correct an expectation formed before the employee learns the applicable limit.

section: Diagnose the failure before changing the process
objective: Recognise useful improvement of a necessary control
stem: A supplier-payment team verifies that goods arrived before releasing payment. The check addresses a material risk, but missing delivery records cause delays. What does the Hammer test support?

options.text: Remove the check because it creates a handoff and therefore wastes time.
options.rationale: A handoff is not automatically waste; this check serves a stated control purpose.

options.text: Improve receipt information so the necessary check can be completed reliably and promptly.
options.rationale: Useful improvement can preserve a necessary step while reducing delay caused by poor information.

options.text: Keep the delay because a step that controls risk should not be changed.
options.rationale: A necessary control can still be made more reliable or timely.

options.text: Replace the check with a faster payment screen without changing receipt information.
options.rationale: A faster interface does not supply the evidence needed to verify delivery.

section: Draw a should-be process
objective: Define an evidence-based exception route in a simplified process
stem: An insurer’s proposed photo-based claim process receives blurry pictures that do not establish the damage. What should the process provide?

options.text: A route to obtain adequate evidence, including an inspection when needed.
options.rationale: The simplified route is appropriate only when the evidence is sufficient; unclear cases need another path.

options.text: Automatic approval because photo submission satisfies the new process.
options.rationale: Receiving a photograph is not the same as establishing the loss.

options.text: Automatic rejection because every customer must complete the same photo route.
options.rationale: An exception may need different evidence; an inadequate image alone does not establish that the claim is invalid.

options.text: Payment based on the average of previous claims with similar filenames.
options.rationale: Averages and filenames do not establish the loss or its coverage under the policy.

section: Draw a should-be process
objective: Separate end-to-end ownership from unrestricted payment authority
stem: A company assigns one coordinator to keep employees informed throughout reimbursement. A designer therefore gives that coordinator unrestricted authority to calculate and release every payment. What is the design error?

options.text: An end-to-end contact cannot work with specialist reviewers.
options.rationale: A single point of contact can retain responsibility while involving specialists.

options.text: Every reimbursement must be approved personally by the chief executive.
options.rationale: The chapter does not prescribe a universal approver; authority depends on the relevant control rules.

options.text: Responsibility for the experience does not by itself establish authority to release payments.
options.rationale: Payment authority and required checks must be defined rather than inferred from case ownership.

options.text: A coordinator should be responsible only until the employee submits the form.
options.rationale: That boundary would abandon the end-to-end responsibility the company intended to establish.

section: Draw a should-be process
objective: Preserve verification while simplifying a customer-facing process
stem: A retailer wants one help-desk employee to handle an account-recovery request from start to finish. The proposed shortcut removes identity checks because transferring the call is unpopular. Which redesign best addresses both concerns?

options.text: Restore all previous transfers even when they contribute no verification.
options.rationale: Keeping every transfer preserves burden without showing which work controls the risk.

options.text: Use a polite explanation in place of verifying the requester’s identity.
options.rationale: Clear communication cannot establish that the requester is entitled to the account.

options.text: Reset the account immediately and investigate identity only if someone complains.
options.rationale: This removes the preventive check and may allow an unauthorised person access before review.

options.text: Keep an accountable contact, perform required verification and escalate cases beyond that person’s authority.
options.rationale: Ownership can improve the experience while evidence and escalation protect against improper access.

section: Test the proposed experience
objective: Identify a customer benefit that does not require a larger settlement
stem: In the proposed fence process, the customer still receives $700 but learns the settlement basis earlier and avoids taking an afternoon off. Which conclusion is supported?

options.text: The experience can improve even though the settlement amount stays the same.
options.rationale: Earlier understanding and reduced customer effort are benefits distinct from the payment amount.

options.text: The experience cannot improve unless the insurer pays more than $700.
options.rationale: This treats the amount as the only outcome and ignores effort and uncertainty.

options.text: The unchanged payment proves the insurer’s total processing cost is unchanged.
options.rationale: An identical settlement says nothing about staff time, inspection costs or correction work.

options.text: The avoided visit proves photo evidence is sufficient for every claim.
options.rationale: A workable route for a straightforward case does not establish adequacy for all cases.

section: Test the proposed experience
objective: Recognise when internal savings transfer work to the customer of a process
stem: Finance saves five minutes per expense report by asking employees to copy their entries into a second form. Employees spend eight extra minutes doing so. With all other work unchanged, how should the manager interpret this?

options.text: The redesign saves five minutes overall because finance owns the process.
options.rationale: Ownership does not make employee time disappear from the complete process.

options.text: The redesign saves thirteen minutes overall by combining both figures.
options.rationale: The employee’s eight minutes are added effort, not another saving.

options.text: Finance’s local saving creates a net increase of three minutes across the process.
options.rationale: Eight added minutes minus five saved minutes means three more minutes of work overall.

options.text: The two figures cannot be compared unless both people work in finance.
options.rationale: Both measure time per report; different roles do not prevent comparing the total work.

section: Decide whether the redesign deserves to survive
objective: Select a fair comparison for a narrow redesign pilot
stem: An insurer pilots photo review on simple low-value fence claims during a quiet month. Which comparison would best help judge the new process?

options.text: All complex claims from the previous year’s largest storm.
options.rationale: Claim complexity and workload differ substantially, making the process effect hard to isolate.

options.text: Similar eligible claims using the current process with reasonably comparable staffing and storm volume.
options.rationale: A comparable case group and operating conditions make the comparison more informative.

options.text: Only new-process claims that settled without any exception.
options.rationale: Selecting easy successes removes precisely the cases that could reveal problems.

options.text: The fastest claim ever completed by either process.
options.rationale: An extreme case does not represent typical performance or control risk.

section: Decide whether the redesign deserves to survive
objective: Define a time measure from the customer’s endpoint
stem: A shop reports “repairs completed in two days” because the technician finishes on day 2. Customers receive their items on day 6. Which measure answers how long customers wait for the repaired item?

options.text: Time from technician assignment to repair completion.
options.rationale: This excludes time before assignment and after technical work is finished.

options.text: Time from invoice creation to payment by the customer.
options.rationale: This measures the billing interval, not receipt of the repaired item.

options.text: Time from repair completion to the manager’s approval.
options.rationale: This measures only one internal interval and may still end before customer receipt.

options.text: Time from the customer’s fault report to the customer’s receipt of the repaired item.
options.rationale: The start and finish match the customer-facing outcome being evaluated.

section: Decide whether the redesign deserves to survive
objective: Include costs shifted into correction and support when evaluating a redesign
stem: An automated registration pilot reduces processing time but increases manual corrections and adviser calls. Which cost measure best supports a decision about expansion?

options.text: Total cost per correctly completed registration, including correction and support work.
options.rationale: This includes the extra work needed to deliver the intended outcome rather than pricing only the automated step.

options.text: Software fee per submitted registration, excluding work done by advisers.
options.rationale: This leaves out costs the pilot may have shifted to staff.

options.text: Cost per automatic approval, omitting records that require correction.
options.rationale: Excluding problem cases can make the new process appear cheaper than it is.

options.text: Total adviser cost without counting software or processing work.
options.rationale: Adviser workload matters, but that measure alone excludes other relevant resources.

section: Decide whether the redesign deserves to survive
objective: Choose revision rather than automatic expansion or rejection when pilot results are mixed
stem: A repair pilot’s early status updates reduce repeat customer calls. Remote diagnosis, however, causes an unacceptable number of wrong parts to be ordered. What response best follows the chapter’s pilot logic?

options.text: Expand both changes because fewer calls prove the pilot succeeded.
options.rationale: One useful outcome does not cancel an unacceptable error rate elsewhere in the process.

options.text: Discard the status updates because any failed element invalidates every change.
options.rationale: The results distinguish a useful element from one that needs revision.

options.text: Retain the useful updates, restrict remote diagnosis and test a revised evidence rule.
options.rationale: A pilot can support keeping a benefit while revising the part that fails the control or quality test.

options.text: Continue unchanged until staff become accustomed to the error rate.
options.rationale: An unacceptable error rate calls for a response, not acceptance through familiarity.

section: Naming what you just did
objective: Distinguish an as-is map from a should-be map
stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes an as-is map from a should-be map?

options.text: The as-is map shows the policy manual; the should-be map shows actual practice.
options.rationale: An as-is map should be checked against actual work rather than treated as a copy of the manual.

options.text: The as-is map describes the current process; the should-be map proposes a future process.
options.rationale: One is the best supported account of current work; the other is a design to test.

options.text: The as-is map contains people; the should-be map contains only software.
options.rationale: Both maps may include people, technology, decisions and responsibilities.

options.text: The as-is map includes exceptions; the should-be map removes all exceptions.
options.rationale: A proposed process still needs routes for cases that cannot safely follow its ordinary path.

section: Naming what you just did
objective: Interpret a lane crossing in a swimlane map
stem: What does an arrow crossing from one role’s swimlane into another normally represent?

options.text: A handoff of work or information between roles.
options.rationale: The lanes identify responsibility, so a crossing shows work or information passing to someone else.

options.text: A change from the current process to the proposed process.
options.rationale: A lane boundary separates roles within a map, not current and future designs.

options.text: Evidence that the previous step must be removed.
options.rationale: A handoff is worth examining but may provide a necessary specialist review or control.

options.text: A confirmed delay of at least one working day.
options.rationale: A crossing identifies a transfer; its waiting time requires evidence.

section: Naming what you just did
objective: Identify work whose original purpose has disappeared
stem: Employees used to copy approved expenses into finance’s separate system. The systems now share the approved record automatically, but finance still requires the copy solely to transfer those same fields. What should the redesign examine?

options.text: How to type the copied fields faster while retaining both entries.
options.rationale: This accelerates work whose stated transfer purpose may already be met.

options.text: How to reward staff for completing more duplicate entries.
options.rationale: The measure encourages the activity without checking whether it remains necessary.

options.text: How to keep the copy permanently because it was once a sensible step.
options.rationale: A useful historical reason does not establish a continuing purpose after the systems change.

options.text: Whether the shared record makes copying unnecessary while approval and payment checks remain intact.
options.rationale: The Hammer test asks whether the original reason for the work has disappeared without discarding other controls.

section: Your turn
objective: Specify a workable exception path that preserves protection against improper payment
stem: An employee’s reimbursement request lacks a receipt. The normal process checks the receipt and checks for duplicate payment. Which exception path is best specified?

options.text: Send the request and available evidence to an authorised reviewer; record the decision and retain the duplicate-payment check.
options.rationale: The exception has evidence, decision authority and a retained control against paying the same expense twice.

options.text: Approve any request labelled urgent and check duplicates only after payment.
options.rationale: Urgency does not establish entitlement, and moving the duplicate check loses its preventive role.

options.text: Return the request to the employee every day until a receipt appears, with no review route.
options.rationale: Repeating the normal requirement provides no decision path for a case that cannot satisfy it.

options.text: Forward it to a general mailbox without naming who may approve an alternative.
options.rationale: A destination alone does not establish responsibility or authority to resolve the exception.

section: A question from a three-year-old
objective: Distinguish the customer benefit from the product that supplies it
stem: A photography firm assumes customers will continue buying its instant-print cameras because they still want to see pictures immediately. What does that reasoning overlook?

options.text: Customers must stop valuing immediate viewing when a new camera appears.
options.rationale: A new product can satisfy an existing need; the need does not have to disappear.

options.text: Another product may deliver immediate viewing without requiring the same camera or supplies.
options.rationale: The desired benefit can remain while customers change how they obtain it.

options.text: A familiar customer need makes the existing product cheaper to manufacture.
options.rationale: Continued demand for the benefit does not establish any reduction in production cost.

options.text: A new product can compete only by creating a completely different customer need.
options.rationale: Different products can compete to deliver the same benefit.

section: A question from a three-year-old
objective: Distinguish recognising a technology from building a viable response
stem: A photography firm has demonstrated a digital prototype, but customers are adopting competing products faster than it can establish a workable offering. Which conclusion is best supported?

options.text: The prototype proves that the firm’s commercial transition has succeeded.
options.rationale: Technical awareness and a demonstration do not establish a viable offering customers will buy.

options.text: The slow transition proves the firm never recognised the technology.
options.rationale: The prototype is evidence of recognition; the difficulty lies in turning capability into a business response.

options.text: The firm can postpone customer adoption until its own transition is ready.
options.rationale: The organisation cannot set the timetable on which competing alternatives become attractive.

options.text: Recognition is established, but a viable response must still meet a market timetable the firm does not control.
options.rationale: The firm can see the change without yet having an offering capable of competing as customers move.

section: The mechanism, and where you have seen it before
objective: Identify an intermediary function that survives cheaper search
stem: A company’s employees can now compare flight prices directly. They still rely on a travel service to rearrange disrupted international trips. What should a manager ask before cancelling that service?

options.text: Whether the value of disruption assistance still justifies its cost after search becomes easier.
options.rationale: Cheaper search does not remove the separate work of handling difficult or disrupted travel.

options.text: Whether any employee can find a fare online, since that settles the need for the service.
options.rationale: Finding a fare establishes search capability, not the ability to resolve disrupted trips.

options.text: Whether the travel service’s website has more search filters than the airlines’ sites.
options.rationale: Search features alone do not assess the assistance employees still use.

options.text: Whether the travel service can keep its old fee without describing its remaining work.
options.rationale: The fee needs justification in the functions that remain useful, not only in past practice.

section: A company built around the opportunity
objective: Calculate exchange connections under stated all-to-all assumptions
stem: Assume every one of four buyers needs access to every one of three sellers. Direct connections are counted once per buyer–seller pair. With an exchange, each participant needs one link to it. What are the two counts?

options.text: 7 direct links and 12 exchange links.
options.rationale: This reverses the models: direct buyer–seller pairs require multiplication, while participant-to-exchange links require addition.

options.text: 12 direct links and 4 exchange links.
options.rationale: Four counts only the buyers’ exchange links and omits the three sellers.

options.text: 12 direct links and 7 exchange links.
options.rationale: Four times three gives 12 direct links; four plus three gives seven links to the exchange.

options.text: 7 direct links and 7 exchange links.
options.rationale: Adding participants gives the exchange count, not the number of all-to-all buyer–seller pairs.

section: A company built around the opportunity
objective: Reject a comparison between acquisition price and industry annual revenue
stem: A forecast predicts $20 million in annual booking-fee revenue across the hotel-platform industry. One hotel marketplace is later acquired for $80 million. An analyst calls this a $60 million forecast underestimate. What is the central problem?

options.text: Acquisition prices can never provide information about a business.
options.rationale: An acquisition price is an outcome, but it measures a different thing from annual industry revenue.

options.text: The comparison mixes one company’s valuation with an industry’s annual revenue.
options.rationale: The quantities and populations differ; a comparable outcome within the forecast’s horizon is needed.

options.text: The analyst should divide $80 million by $20 million and report a fourfold success.
options.rationale: Changing the arithmetic does not fix the mismatch in what the numbers measure.

options.text: Any acquisition proves that the entire industry forecast was too optimistic.
options.rationale: A sale does not by itself establish failure of a capability or an industry-wide forecast.

section: A forecast is several claims joined together
objective: Distinguish order-count adoption from spending-value adoption
stem: A marketplace forecast assumes half of purchasing spending will move online. A survey finds that half of orders are online, but those orders account for only 15% of spending. What does the survey support?

options.text: The forecast is confirmed because both statements contain the word “half.”
options.rationale: The same percentage applied to different measures does not establish the same result.

options.text: Half of the spending is online if enough small orders are counted.
options.rationale: Counting more orders does not change their combined share of spending.

options.text: Online adoption has failed because the spending share is below the order share.
options.rationale: The figures show different adoption shares by measure, not that adoption has failed altogether.

options.text: Half of orders are online, but the forecast’s spending assumption is not established by that figure.
options.rationale: Order counts and dollar value must be assessed separately; the measured spending share is 15%.

section: A forecast is several claims joined together
objective: Identify the reachable population behind a market-size assumption
stem: A presenter uses total annual hospital purchasing to size a marketplace that can currently handle only standard office supplies. Which revision would make the market assumption more defensible?

options.text: Identify purchasing categories and spending the service can realistically handle.
options.rationale: The relevant reachable market may be much smaller than the institution’s total purchases.

options.text: Count all hospital spending but lower the website’s operating-cost estimate.
options.rationale: A lower cost estimate does not make unsuitable purchases reachable.

options.text: Replace spending with the number of hospital employees.
options.rationale: Employee count is a different measure and does not establish eligible purchasing volume.

options.text: Include other industries to make the total market large enough for the target revenue.
options.rationale: Expanding the total without testing suitability compounds the unsupported assumption.

section: A forecast is several claims joined together
objective: Calculate fee revenue from market size, adoption, share and fee
stem: In a hypothetical annual forecast, eligible purchases total $200 million. Forty percent move online, a marketplace handles 25% of that online value and collects a 2% fee. What is its annual fee revenue before costs?

options.text: $4 million.
options.rationale: Two percent of the entire $200 million ignores both online adoption and the marketplace’s share.

options.text: $20 million.
options.rationale: This is the transaction value handled: $200 million × 40% × 25%. It is not fee revenue.
The marketplace handles $20 million of purchases and earns 2% of that value, or $400,000.

options.text: $1.6 million.
options.rationale: This applies the fee to all $80 million of online purchasing and omits the marketplace’s 25% share.

section: A forecast is several claims joined together
objective: Distinguish marketplace revenue from profit
stem: A marketplace states its annual fee revenue. Which further quantity is needed to determine its profit from providing that service?

options.text: The total value of goods purchased through it.
options.rationale: Transaction value is not the marketplace’s cost and cannot simply be subtracted to determine service profit.

options.text: The costs of supplying the service that earned the revenue.
options.rationale: Profit requires accounting for the resources consumed in supplying the service, not just the fees earned.

options.text: The last price offered to acquire the company.
options.rationale: An acquisition offer concerns company valuation, not the period’s service costs.

options.text: The number of links shown in its exchange diagram.
options.rationale: A connection count does not measure the actual costs of providing the service.

section: Your second instrument
objective: State the direction–destination distinction
stem: In the FreeMarkets test, what does “destination” refer to?

options.text: Who captures the value, through what arrangement and for how long.
options.rationale: Destination concerns the distribution and durability of benefits from an adopted capability.

options.text: The capability people adopt and the behaviour it changes.
options.rationale: That is the direction side of the test.

options.text: The physical place where goods are delivered.
options.rationale: The term describes value capture here, not a shipment’s endpoint.

options.text: The maximum number of participants a website can support.
options.rationale: Technical capacity does not establish who benefits economically from use.

section: Your second instrument
objective: Identify adoption requirements that a narrow demonstration leaves untested
stem: A marketplace demonstrates bids on identical boxes. A manufacturer needs customised packaging recorded in its own purchasing system. What should it investigate before treating the demonstration as adoption evidence?

options.text: Whether the demonstration can attract even more bids on the identical boxes.
options.rationale: More bids on the same simple case leave the custom requirements and record connection untested.

options.text: Whether the demonstration’s lowest price is below any previous packaging price.
options.rationale: Prices for different specifications do not establish suitability or adoption readiness.

options.text: Whether the vendor describes the product as suitable for every manufacturer.
options.rationale: A broad assertion is not evidence that this firm can specify, connect and use the service.

options.text: Whether custom requirements can be compared consistently, records connected and staff able to use the process.
options.rationale: Adoption depends on the purchasing arrangement, data and people, not only on a working bidding screen.

section: Your second instrument
objective: Evaluate a timing mismatch between eventual adoption and business survival
stem: A marketplace needs fee-paying customers within six months to cover its bills. Interested buyers estimate eighteen months to connect records and change contracts. What is the managerial implication?

options.text: Buyer interest guarantees the marketplace can cover the first year’s bills.
options.rationale: Interest does not supply fee revenue before customers can use and pay for the service.

options.text: The longer integration period proves that online purchasing has no value.
options.rationale: A useful capability can take time to adopt; delay does not establish worthlessness.

options.text: Eventual demand may be real while the current spending and revenue timetable is unworkable.
options.rationale: The business needs a feasible path through the interval before paying adoption occurs.

options.text: The forecast can treat expressions of interest as completed transactions.
options.rationale: Interest and paid use are different events; relabelling them does not solve the cash timing problem.

section: Work through the decision
objective: Make bids comparable before interpreting a lower price
stem: A packaging auction returns one bid for thicker boxes delivered next week and another for thinner boxes delivered next month. The second price is lower. What should the buyer do before calling it a saving?

options.text: Establish comparable quantity, quality and delivery requirements and check supplier eligibility.
options.rationale: A price difference does not establish savings when the offers may fulfil different requirements.

options.text: Accept the second bid because the auction has ranked the prices.
options.rationale: A price ranking cannot decide whether different specifications satisfy the same need.

options.text: Average the prices and use the result as evidence of a saving.
options.rationale: Averaging unlike offers does not make them comparable or establish an acceptable delivered outcome.

options.text: Select the supplier that placed its bid first.
options.rationale: Bid timing does not establish quality, suitability or total cost.

section: Work through the decision
objective: Compare complete purchase costs rather than quoted prices
stem: Assume two packaging options deliver acceptable goods on the required date. The existing route costs $10,000 in total. The auction route costs $9,200 for goods, $200 in fees, $300 in staff preparation and $500 for delivery, with no other costs. What is the comparison?

options.text: The auction saves $800.
options.rationale: This compares only the goods price with the existing total and omits $1,000 in other auction-route costs.

options.text: The auction costs $200 more.
options.rationale: The auction total is $9,200 + $200 + $300 + $500 = $10,200, compared with $10,000.

options.text: The auction costs exactly the same.
options.rationale: The listed auction costs add to $10,200, not $10,000.

options.text: The auction saves $600.
options.rationale: This includes the fee but omits staff preparation and delivery.

section: Work through the decision
objective: Choose a limited test that improves evidence before a large commitment
stem: A hotel group is considering replacing its uniform-purchasing system with a marketplace. It has seen a successful demonstration but has not placed an order. Which next step best fits the chapter’s approach?

options.text: Replace every purchasing category before testing so staff cannot return to the old process.
options.rationale: This expands commitment before establishing acceptable delivery and complete costs.

options.text: Measure how many staff watched the demonstration before approving the replacement.
options.rationale: Attention to the demonstration does not test the actual purchase outcome.

options.text: Defer every decision until the marketplace can guarantee permanent savings.
options.rationale: A limited purchase can provide useful evidence without requiring certainty about every future outcome.

options.text: Test a well-specified uniform order and compare accepted delivery and full cost with a suitable recent purchase.
options.rationale: A bounded test checks the business outcome while limiting the scale of the initial commitment.

section: Work through the decision
objective: Assess separate participation and fee assumptions when adoption holds
stem: A forecast expects a marketplace to handle $60 million annually at a 2% fee. Online purchasing grows as predicted, but the marketplace handles only $30 million and can charge 1%. Which conclusion follows?

options.text: Revenue is $600,000 because only the transaction-volume shortfall matters.
options.rationale: This retains the old 2% fee and ignores the fee reduction.

options.text: Revenue is $600,000 because only the fee reduction matters.
options.rationale: This retains the old $60 million transaction volume and ignores the participation shortfall.

options.text: Revenue is $300,000, one-quarter of the forecast, despite the broader adoption forecast holding.
options.rationale: Expected revenue was $1.2 million; $30 million × 1% is $300,000. Direction can hold while destination disappoints.

options.text: Revenue is unchanged because online purchasing grew as predicted.
options.rationale: Industry adoption does not guarantee this firm’s transaction share or fee.

section: Work through the decision
objective: Distinguish evidence for one customer purchase from evidence for scaling a service
stem: A uniform marketplace completes one pilot order that saves a hotel money. Its founder wants to hire a large sales team immediately. What evidence would most directly strengthen the case for expansion?

options.text: Repeat purchases at fees customers continue to accept, alongside the cost of serving those purchases.
options.rationale: A useful first purchase does not establish repeat demand or viable service economics at scale.

options.text: More photographs of the successful pilot delivery for the sales presentation.
options.rationale: Photographs document the pilot but do not establish recurring paid use or service costs.

options.text: A larger estimate of total hotel spending without checking which purchases fit the service.
options.rationale: A broad market total does not show reachable demand, repeat use or profitable delivery.

options.text: An agreement that the pilot customer may use the marketplace indefinitely without fees.
options.rationale: Free continued access may show interest but does not establish willingness to pay the forecast fee.

section: The middleman changes shape
objective: Recognise removal and replacement of intermediary functions
stem: An artisan stops using a sales agent and opens a direct website. Later, the artisan joins a marketplace for customer discovery and dispute handling. How should a manager interpret these changes?

options.text: Opening the website makes every future intermediary unnecessary.
options.rationale: Direct selling does not remove the need to be found, trusted or supported when disputes arise.

options.text: One intermediary was removed, and another became useful through a different set of functions.
options.rationale: Disintermediation and reintermediation can occur together as the work needed around a transaction changes.

options.text: Joining the marketplace proves the direct website could never accept an order.
options.rationale: The website may function technically while the marketplace provides other useful services.

options.text: The two changes cancel each other, leaving the business arrangement unchanged.
options.rationale: The route and functions have changed even though some intermediation remains.

section: The middleman changes shape
objective: Identify the mechanism of a network effect
stem: As more suitable artisans join a marketplace, buyers find more relevant products. More purchasing buyers then make joining attractive to additional artisans. What makes this a network effect?

options.text: The marketplace installed a faster network connection.
options.rationale: A faster connection is technical performance; the described benefit comes from participation.

options.text: The marketplace reduced every seller’s subscription fee.
options.rationale: No fee reduction is stated, and the mechanism does not depend on one.

options.text: Every additional seller is guaranteed a profitable business.
options.rationale: Greater participation can increase value without guaranteeing each seller’s profit.

options.text: Participation on each side increases the service’s value to participants on the other side.
options.rationale: Relevant sellers attract buyers, and purchasing buyers make the service more valuable to sellers.

section: The middleman changes shape
objective: Evaluate participation quality and transaction leakage rather than size alone
stem: A travel marketplace doubles its listed providers, but many cannot serve the routes buyers need. Customers often use it to find a provider and then book directly. Why is participant growth weak evidence of durable fee revenue?

options.text: Relevant supply and repeat paid transactions matter; listings alone establish neither.
options.rationale: Unsuitable providers add little value, and transactions made outside the marketplace may not generate its fees.

options.text: Doubling the listings must halve the fee revenue.
options.rationale: No fixed relationship between listing count and revenue is established.

options.text: Direct booking proves that the marketplace provided no discovery value.
options.rationale: Customers may gain discovery value without continuing to pay the marketplace for transactions.

options.text: A large participant count guarantees fees once the website becomes faster.
options.rationale: Website speed does not resolve supply relevance or customers’ ability to transact elsewhere.

section: The version you may meet next
objective: Distinguish supplier-comparison assistance from delegated purchasing
stem: A purchasing assistant compares supplier offers accurately in a demonstration. A manager proposes enabling automatic ordering on that basis. What additional capability needs assessment?

options.text: Whether the assistant can display the same comparison in a different colour.
options.rationale: Presentation changes do not address the added authority and consequences of ordering.

options.text: Whether the comparison can be repeated without changing the supplier list.
options.rationale: Repeating advice does not establish safe authority to spend or correct mistaken purchases.

options.text: Whether spending limits, decision authority, records and reversal of mistakes are workable.
options.rationale: Placing orders is delegated action with consequences beyond producing a comparison.

options.text: Whether the demonstration attracted more viewers than an earlier one.
options.rationale: Audience size does not establish readiness to delegate purchasing decisions.

section: The version you may meet next
objective: Identify an open value-capture question after a useful capability is adopted
stem: Purchasing staff widely adopt automated supplier comparisons. A start-up concludes that this guarantees demand for its separate paid assistant, although existing purchasing software now includes comparisons. What remains to be tested?

options.text: Whether any staff use automated comparisons at all.
options.rationale: Adoption is given in the scenario; it does not settle who captures the benefit.

options.text: Why customers would keep paying the start-up rather than use the feature they already have.
options.rationale: The destination claim needs evidence of the start-up’s paid role despite available alternatives.

options.text: Whether widespread adoption forces existing software providers to remove their comparison feature.
options.rationale: No such consequence follows from adoption.

options.text: Whether lower search effort means every provider can charge the same profitable fee.
options.rationale: A useful capability does not guarantee a fee or margin to every provider.

section: Your turn
objective: Identify missing scope and timing without inventing a forecaster’s claim
stem: A dated report says, “Most businesses will buy through digital marketplaces,” but defines neither the business population nor a deadline. What should a student do when preparing to assess it?

options.text: Assume it means all businesses within three years because that makes the forecast testable.
options.rationale: This would add a population and deadline the source did not state.

options.text: Use whichever population shows the strongest adoption at the time of review.
options.rationale: Selecting scope after seeing results changes the claim rather than assessing it fairly.

options.text: Treat the publication date as the forecast’s completion deadline.
options.rationale: The date of publication is not necessarily the date by which the prediction should occur.

options.text: Save the exact claim, identify the missing scope and deadline, and label any proposed interpretation separately.
options.rationale: Missing definitions limit fair evaluation; they should be exposed rather than silently supplied.

section: Your turn
objective: Treat a forecaster’s interest as a reason to seek independent evidence
stem: A marketplace vendor publishes a forecast of rapid adoption and cites a survey of its own customers. What is the most defensible response?

options.text: Examine the survey’s scope and seek independent evidence while recognising the vendor’s interest.
options.rationale: An interest does not make a claim false, but customer selection and incentives warrant examination.

options.text: Reject the forecast solely because the vendor would benefit if it were believed.
options.rationale: An interested source can make a correct claim; its evidence still needs assessment.

options.text: Accept the forecast because the vendor’s customers are the people most familiar with its product.
options.rationale: Familiar customers may not represent the wider population in the adoption claim.

options.text: Replace the adoption claim with a prediction that this vendor will earn the highest profit.
options.rationale: That invents a destination claim rather than assessing the forecast provided.

section: Fifteen months later
objective: Distinguish workload equivalence from a staffing outcome
stem: A retailer reports that its assistant completed work equivalent to 50 full-time agents. What does that statement alone establish?

options.text: Fifty employees were dismissed.
options.rationale: A staffing change needs evidence beyond an equivalence in work.

options.text: A reported amount of work comparable to that of 50 agents, under the company’s calculation.
options.rationale: Equivalence describes capacity or workload; its method and staffing consequences need separate examination.

options.text: Payroll fell by the cost of fifty salaries.
options.rationale: Released time may be redeployed rather than removed from payroll.

options.text: The assistant made fewer mistakes than fifty agents.
options.rationale: A workload measure does not establish accuracy.

section: What kind of claim is it?
objective: Recognise a projection among reported performance measures
stem: Which statement is a projection rather than a report of activity or an observed service result?

options.text: The service handled 8,000 chats last month.
options.rationale: This reports an activity count for a past period.

options.text: Average response time was three minutes during the trial.
options.rationale: This reports a measured time, though its definition still matters.

options.text: Reviewers found that 90 of 100 trial cases met the stated resolution standard.
options.rationale: This reports an observed trial result.

options.text: The service is expected to improve next year’s profit by $200,000.
options.rationale: This is a forecast of a future financial result.

section: What the system is being asked to do
objective: Distinguish employee augmentation from automation of sending
stem: A travel-service assistant drafts a customer reply. An employee checks it against the booking and sends it. How is the assistant used in this arrangement?

options.text: To augment the employee’s work.
options.rationale: The employee remains responsible for checking and carrying out the response task.

options.text: To automate sending without human review.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly retains an employee’s review and sending step.

options.text: To act directly on the booking by issuing a refund.
options.rationale: Drafting a reply does not establish authority to change the booking or issue money.

options.text: To estimate which booking will be cancelled.
options.rationale: The described task produces content rather than estimates that outcome.

section: What the system is being asked to do
objective: Specify authority and escalation when an assistant can act
stem: A retailer proposes allowing an agent to initiate refunds rather than only draft explanations. Which additional design decision is essential?

options.text: Which tone makes the refund message sound most confident.
options.rationale: Tone does not define authority to make a financial commitment.

options.text: How to remove every employee from exception handling.
options.rationale: Uncertain actions still need a defined destination.

options.text: What actions are permitted, which need approval and where failed or uncertain actions go.
options.rationale: Acting changes records or commitments, requiring explicit limits and handling.

options.text: Whether a fluent answer can substitute for checking the order record.
