options.rationale: Fluency does not authorise a refund or establish its correctness.

section: Put a number on a complete outcome
objective: Compare cost per contact with cost per correct resolution
stem: A retailer’s current service costs $900 for 100 cases and correctly resolves 90. A pilot costs $800 for 100 cases and correctly resolves 80, using the same review criteria and period. What follows?

options.text: The pilot proves better service because cost per case falls from $9 to $8.
options.rationale: The cheaper contact figure omits the decline in correct resolutions.

options.text: Both cost $10 per correct resolution; the pilot leaves more cases unresolved or incorrect.
options.rationale: $900/90 and $800/80 both equal $10, so the lower per-case cost does not establish improvement.

options.text: The pilot costs $8 per correct resolution.
options.rationale: That divides by all cases rather than correctly resolved cases.

options.text: The current service has a higher error rate because it spends more.
options.rationale: The supplied results show fewer failures in the current service; spending alone does not determine errors.

section: What the system is being asked to do
objective: Check generated claims against authoritative records despite fluent wording
stem: A travel assistant reads a booking record and produces a polished explanation of a cancellation deadline. What review remains necessary?

options.text: Only checking spelling because access to the record guarantees agreement.
options.rationale: Record access does not ensure the generated answer accurately represents it.

options.text: Replacing hesitant language with confident wording.
options.rationale: Confidence of tone does not supply evidence of correctness.

options.text: Checking only whether the customer likes the explanation.
options.rationale: A pleasing explanation may still misstate the deadline.

options.text: Check the stated deadline against the booking and applicable policy.
options.rationale: The result must agree with the relevant record and rule, even when the model could access them.

section: Put a number on a complete outcome
objective: Treat abandoned interactions as unresolved evidence
stem: Some travel customers abandon a service pilot before their booking problem is resolved. How should the team handle those cases?

options.text: Retain them as unresolved evidence and investigate why customers stopped.
options.rationale: Leaving the interaction does not demonstrate resolution.

options.text: Count them as resolved because they did not request more help.
options.rationale: Silence can reflect giving up rather than successful service.

options.text: Drop them so only completed interactions affect the results.
options.rationale: Excluding difficult cases can inflate apparent performance.

options.text: Count them as confirmed system failures without examining the reason.
options.rationale: The cases are unresolved evidence; investigation is needed to understand what happened.

section: The other number
objective: Avoid converting unlike report measures into a project failure probability
stem: A preliminary report describes organisations reporting no return and, separately, integrated pilots producing value. It notes selection limits and different success definitions. What can a travel manager infer about a proposed local pilot?

options.text: The organisation-level percentage is its exact probability of pilot failure.
options.rationale: The measures and sampled population do not establish that probability.

options.text: The report must be false if one company reports success.
options.rationale: A broad pattern and a particular success can coexist.

options.text: The report raises questions to test locally but does not supply a universal failure probability.
options.rationale: Different units and limited methods constrain what the headline establishes.

options.text: Its limitations mean every result can be ignored.
options.rationale: Limited evidence may still guide useful questions without settling the decision.

section: Put a number on a complete outcome
objective: Define a credible pilot before evaluating its result
stem: A travel manager is approving a service pilot. Which specification best supports a defensible comparison?

options.text: A target chat count and the model’s advertised price only.
options.rationale: Activity and one fee omit quality, comparison and full cost.

options.text: Comparable eligible cases and review periods, a complete resolution standard, full costs and a condition for stopping or narrowing.
options.rationale: These define what success means and how evidence will affect the decision.

options.text: A satisfaction survey only for customers whose cases the assistant closes.
options.rationale: That excludes other assigned cases and cannot establish the complete outcome.

options.text: A comparison of the pilot’s easy cases with the old service’s entire workload.
options.rationale: Different case mixes can create a misleading performance difference.

section: Both instruments, on one case
objective: Separate a useful copied capability from durable advantage
stem: A retailer’s assistant reliably resolves routine questions, but rivals can reproduce the capability cheaply. What does this establish about lasting advantage?

options.text: Customer use alone proves an advantage rivals cannot match.
options.rationale: Adoption does not establish durable differentiation.

options.text: The improvement has no business value because it can be copied.
options.rationale: Better service can be valuable or necessary without creating a lasting edge.

options.text: The AI label itself establishes that the retailer keeps the benefit.
options.rationale: Technology type does not settle who captures value.

options.text: Useful adoption is plausible, but a durable advantage requires further evidence about value capture and what rivals cannot match.
options.rationale: Direction of adoption and destination of the benefit remain separate questions.

section: What kind of claim is it?
objective: Recognise concurrent changes before attributing a result to AI
stem: A retailer’s response times fall after it introduces an assistant, simplifies its returns policy and receives fewer complex enquiries. What is unresolved?

options.text: How much of the improvement was caused by the assistant rather than the other changes.
options.rationale: A before-and-after result with concurrent changes cannot isolate the assistant’s contribution.

options.text: Whether any improvement occurred at all, even though measured times fell.
options.rationale: The cause is uncertain; that does not erase the reported time difference.

options.text: Whether the simpler policy proves the assistant had no effect.
options.rationale: Several changes may contribute; the scenario does not establish zero contribution.

options.text: Whether every reduction in time automatically improves correctness.
options.rationale: Time and correctness are separate, and neither resolves the causal question.

section: What the system is being asked to do
objective: Distinguish predicting an outcome from generating content
stem: Which pair correctly distinguishes the business tasks of prediction and generation?

options.text: Prediction: drafting an email; generation: estimating a delay probability.
options.rationale: This reverses the task distinction used in the chapter.

options.text: Prediction: approving a refund; generation: updating the order record.
options.rationale: Both describe actions rather than the stated distinction.

options.text: Prediction: estimating whether a return will be delayed; generation: drafting its explanation.
options.rationale: Prediction estimates an outcome; generation produces content.

options.text: Prediction and generation both necessarily act in another business system.
options.rationale: Neither task alone implies authority to change a record or commitment.

section: Put a number on a complete outcome
objective: Keep escalated cases within the assigned pilot workload
stem: A retailer’s assistant routes difficult pilot cases to staff. The analyst removes them from the assistant group’s cost and outcome figures. What should change?

options.text: Count every escalation as a failure regardless of whether it was required and completed.
options.rationale: A necessary, completed escalation can be part of a correct resolution.

options.text: Keep all assigned cases and include the staff work and eventual outcomes.
options.rationale: Otherwise the pilot receives credit for easy cases while its difficult work disappears.

options.text: Move the cases into the comparison group after seeing that they are difficult.
options.rationale: Reassigning cases based on their difficulty distorts the comparison.

options.text: Count the transfer itself as a complete resolution.
options.rationale: Routing is not completion if required follow-up remains unfinished.

section: Both instruments, on one case
objective: Identify a supplier’s capture of an operational saving
stem: A travel service saves $12,000 in annual operating work, but the supplier’s added annual fees are $10,000. Under these simplified figures, what should management recognise?

options.text: The travel service retains all $12,000 because it created the operating improvement.
options.rationale: The extra supplier fee absorbs part of that benefit.

options.text: There is no operational improvement because the supplier charges for it.
options.rationale: The service can improve while the supplier captures much of its value.

options.text: The $10,000 fee is an additional saving to add to $12,000.
options.rationale: The fee is a cost to the travel service.

options.text: Only $2,000 remains before other effects; who captures the value differs from whether the capability helps.
options.rationale: $12,000 minus $10,000 leaves $2,000 under the stated assumptions.

section: Both instruments, on one case
objective: Distinguish customer benefit from evidence of firm profitability
stem: A retailer passes the saving from a better returns service to customers through lower charges. What can it conclude from that change alone?

options.text: Customers receive a benefit; increased retailer profit or lasting advantage needs separate evidence.
options.rationale: Value can reach customers without automatically increasing the retailer’s retained return.

options.text: The retailer necessarily retains the entire saving as profit.
options.rationale: Passing savings on changes who keeps them.

options.text: The improvement is pointless because customers benefit.
options.rationale: Customer benefit can support useful service even without immediate additional profit.

options.text: Lower charges prove competitors cannot imitate the arrangement.
options.rationale: Pricing does not establish barriers to imitation.

section: Both instruments, on one case
objective: Test local use and reliable outcomes before inferring benefit capture
stem: A travel service expects to profit from an assistant because similar tools are popular. Which evidence addresses the direction question for this proposal?

options.text: Only whether the vendor’s shareholders gained value.
options.rationale: That does not show customers using this service successfully.

options.text: Only the number of competing products advertised online.
options.rationale: Supply of products does not establish useful local adoption.

options.text: Whether its customers use the service and their problems are reliably resolved.
options.rationale: The proposal needs evidence that the capability works in this setting before value capture can be assessed.

options.text: A claim that every popular capability must generate profit for every adopter.
options.rationale: Popularity does not establish either local performance or retained return.

section: Hammer walks back in
objective: Choose a process change that prevents an avoidable enquiry
stem: A warehouse reliably records receipt of returns, but customers cannot see that status and repeatedly ask for it. What change could prevent some contacts?

options.text: Hide the contact form so fewer questions reach the service team.
options.rationale: That reduces access without resolving the customer’s information need.

options.text: Make the recorded receipt status available to customers at the relevant step.
options.rationale: The question may cease to be necessary when customers can see reliable information.

options.text: Ask the assistant to give a confident answer without consulting the record.
options.rationale: Confidence cannot replace reliable status information.

options.text: Treat every contact as evidence that returns should be refused.
options.rationale: The stated issue is missing visibility, not invalid returns.

section: Hammer walks back in
objective: Preserve contact that serves judgment or appeal rather than suppress it
stem: A travel customer needs review of an unusual cancellation circumstance. A manager wants to eliminate the contact to improve the contact-reduction metric. What is the better interpretation?

options.text: Every contact is waste because a digital service should require none.
options.rationale: Some contacts provide necessary judgment, explanation or choice.

options.text: Blocking the appeal is process improvement if conversation counts fall.
options.rationale: A lower activity count can hide worse service.

options.text: The assistant should invent a new policy so no person is needed.
options.rationale: Generating text does not confer policy authority.

options.text: This may be a necessary route to judgment; assess resolution quality rather than seek fewer contacts at any cost.
options.rationale: Preventable confusion differs from a request the organisation should make possible.

section: Hammer walks back in
objective: Locate a common record problem inherited by two proposed solutions
stem: A retailer considers automated status replies or a self-service status page, but warehouse receipt entries are often missing. What must the comparison recognise?

options.text: Both approaches depend on improving the unreliable receipt record.
options.rationale: A different interface does not supply information the underlying process failed to record.

options.text: The status page automatically creates accurate warehouse records.
options.rationale: Displaying a record does not correct missing capture.

options.text: The assistant’s fluency makes incomplete records irrelevant.
options.rationale: A fluent answer cannot establish an unrecorded event.

options.text: The two interfaces must have identical implementation costs.
options.rationale: A shared data problem does not establish equal costs.

section: Change the handoff deliberately
objective: Reduce routine handoffs while preserving specialist authority
stem: A travel case owner can retrieve configuration notes and earlier support tickets. A requested arrangement still requires specialist approval. How should the handoff be redesigned?

options.text: Let the owner promise any arrangement because the notes are now available.
options.rationale: Access to information does not supply specialist expertise or authority.

options.text: Keep every routine question moving through all departments regardless of need.
options.rationale: Shared information may allow some unnecessary transfers to be removed.

options.text: Keep routine cases with the owner and route the exceptional commitment to the authorised specialist while retaining customer ownership.
options.rationale: Coordination can improve without eliminating necessary expertise or accountability.

options.text: Judge success solely by the number of specialist roles removed.
options.rationale: Changing roles does not establish better service, quality or cost.

section: Decide what the saved time becomes
objective: Specify the useful destination of released staff capacity
stem: A retailer’s revised pilot releases small amounts of time across many staff members, who remain employed. What should management specify next?

options.text: An automatic payroll saving equal to every minute released.
options.rationale: Dispersed available time does not necessarily reduce payroll.

options.text: How time will support useful work or an observable cost reduction, and who will check that outcome.
options.rationale: Released capacity becomes a benefit through an operational choice and evidence.

options.text: A second benefit equal to the same hours, counted again as extra output and saved wages.
options.rationale: This would double-count the same resource.

options.text: That no benefit can exist unless whole jobs disappear.
options.rationale: The time may support growth, difficult cases or reduced overtime.

section: Decide what the saved time becomes
objective: Reassess unit economics when volume changes
stem: A travel assistant’s monthly cost remains $1,000. Correct resolutions fall from 200 to 100 as demand declines. Under these simplified assumptions, what happens?

options.text: Cost per correct resolution remains $5 because the monthly cost is unchanged.
options.rationale: The denominator has fallen.

options.text: Cost per correct resolution halves because there is less work.
options.rationale: The stated cost does not halve with volume.

options.text: Quality necessarily deteriorated because the count fell.
options.rationale: Lower demand can reduce correct-resolution counts without changing their rate.

options.text: Cost per correct resolution rises from $5 to $10, so the economics need review.
options.rationale: $1,000/200 is $5 and $1,000/100 is $10; a successful high-volume estimate may not hold.

section: Put a number on a complete outcome
objective: Investigate serious errors rather than let a favourable average override a limit
stem: A retailer’s pilot has a strong average result but issues an unauthorised refund, violating a pre-agreed stop condition. What should the decision owner do?

options.text: Apply the stop or narrowing condition, investigate the action controls and require evidence before resuming the affected use.
options.rationale: A favourable average cannot erase a serious failure the organisation agreed was unacceptable.

options.text: Expand because one serious error is outweighed automatically by many correct answers.
options.rationale: The acceptance condition explicitly treats that failure separately.

options.text: Remove the refund case from the sample because it was unusual.
options.rationale: Excluding it would hide the risk the pilot should reveal.

options.text: Conclude that every possible AI use is permanently unsuitable.
options.rationale: The failure calls for action on the affected arrangement, not an unsupported universal conclusion.

section: Decide what the saved time becomes
objective: Assign monitoring and intervention after operating conditions change
stem: A travel assistant passed its pilot, but new policies and booking types now create unfamiliar questions. What arrangement should continue after launch?

options.text: Rely only on the original pilot because approval settled future performance.
options.rationale: Changed conditions can make an earlier configuration unreliable.

options.text: Monitor conversation volume alone and ignore correctness.
options.rationale: Activity does not reveal whether the new work is resolved properly.

options.text: Check outcomes under the new conditions and give an owner authority to change scope, expand or pause.
options.rationale: Monitoring matters when evidence reaches someone able to act on it.

options.text: Keep the scope fixed so employees never need further training.
options.rationale: An unchanged scope is not justified if the work or risks change.

section: The boring thing becomes the business
objective: Diagnose an order error caused by inconsistent units
stem: A hospital requests 12 boxes of gloves. Its software sends the quantity 12 successfully, but the supplier reads it as 12 cases of ten boxes each. Which problem most directly explains the excess delivery?

options.text: The network failed to transmit the quantity.
options.rationale: The stated quantity arrived; the problem concerns how each side interpreted it.

options.text: The systems did not agree on the unit represented by the quantity.
options.rationale: The same number means different amounts when one system uses boxes and the other uses cases.

options.text: The hospital needs a faster ordering screen.
options.rationale: Screen speed does not align the meanings of boxes and cases.

options.text: The supplier needs to increase its warehouse capacity.
options.rationale: Capacity does not correct an order that specifies the wrong amount.

section: The boring thing becomes the business
objective: Assign responsibility for maintaining a shared item mapping
stem: A supplier changes from ten boxes per case to eight. A hospital’s old item mapping remains in use. Which arrangement best prevents continuing quantity errors?

options.text: Retain the original mapping because it was correct when approved.
options.rationale: A previously correct definition can become wrong when packaging changes.

options.text: Ask each ward to guess the conversion when it orders.
options.rationale: Separate guesses create inconsistent meanings rather than an agreed, maintained mapping.

options.text: Rely on a successful connection test to confirm the mapping.
options.rationale: A connection test can establish transmission without checking the current business meaning.

options.text: Assign an owner to verify packaging changes, approve mapping updates and check affected orders.
options.rationale: Shared definitions need a responsible maintenance process when the underlying products change.

section: The boring thing becomes the business
objective: Identify what an API provides
stem: What is an application programming interface, or API, in the chapter’s explanation?

options.text: A defined way for one piece of software to request data or an action from another.
options.rationale: An API provides a specified software interaction; the business still defines correct use and meaning.

options.text: A guarantee that two organisations use identical product definitions.
options.rationale: A connection does not guarantee agreement on item meanings or quantities.

options.text: A contract transferring every ordering decision to the software supplier.
options.rationale: An API does not by itself assign business authority or responsibility.

options.text: A complete purchasing process that requires no exception handling.
options.rationale: An API can support a process, but it does not remove exceptions or the need to handle them.

section: The boring thing becomes the business
objective: Specify safe handling of an uncertain order submission
stem: A retailer submits an order through an API. The confirmation does not arrive, so a clerk considers submitting it again. Which business rule is most important before automatic retries are enabled?

options.text: Retry until a confirmation appears, treating every attempt as a new purchase.
options.rationale: The first request may already have created an order; repeated new purchases could duplicate it.

options.text: Assume that no confirmation means the supplier rejected the order.
options.rationale: The order may have been accepted even though the response was lost or delayed.

options.text: Establish how staff check whether the order exists and how retries avoid a second purchase.
options.rationale: An uncertain response requires a defined checking and repeat-request process to prevent duplicates.

options.text: Increase the order quantity to compensate for possible missing requests.
options.rationale: Changing the quantity does not establish whether the original order succeeded and can increase the error.

section: The boring thing becomes the business
objective: Calculate simple switching payback using transition and recurring costs
stem: Assume a hospital would save $90,000 a year on identical supplies after switching. The change costs $100,000 once and adds $40,000 in annual coordination costs. With constant volumes and prices, ignoring timing and other effects, when do net savings cover the initial work?

options.text: About 1.11 years.
options.rationale: Dividing $100,000 by $90,000 ignores the additional annual coordination cost.

options.text: Two years.
options.rationale: Net annual savings are $90,000 minus $40,000, or $50,000; $100,000 divided by $50,000 is two years.

options.text: Two and a half years.
options.rationale: This divides the initial cost by the new coordination cost rather than the net annual saving.

options.text: The first year.
options.rationale: The first year’s $50,000 net operating saving does not cover $100,000 of initial work.

section: The boring thing becomes the business
objective: Test whether projected switching savings persist long enough
stem: A hospital’s switching calculation breaks even after two years at the offered price. The new supplier guarantees that price for only six months. What follows?

options.text: The decision needs evidence about later prices and whether savings survive that uncertainty.
options.rationale: A two-year calculation relies on savings continuing beyond the six-month guaranteed period.

options.text: The supplier must maintain the same price until the hospital breaks even.
options.rationale: The stated guarantee does not establish that commitment.

options.text: The hospital should count the six-month discount as a permanent annual saving.
options.rationale: This extends a temporary commitment beyond the evidence supplied.

options.text: The switch cannot be worthwhile under any future price.
options.rationale: Uncertainty does not establish inevitable failure; alternative price outcomes need examination.

section: The reversal, and how to reconcile it
objective: Preserve a useful capability while replacing its current software
stem: A club dislikes its membership software, but its checked records of membership categories and fee exceptions are valuable. Which replacement approach best follows the chapter?

options.text: Discard the exception records so the new software starts with simpler data.
options.rationale: Simpler data may lose the knowledge needed to charge members correctly.

options.text: Keep the current software solely because its records are useful.
options.rationale: Useful records do not prove that the same software must continue providing them.

options.text: Choose a new interface before asking whether it can represent the existing categories.
options.rationale: An attractive interface does not establish that the replacement can preserve the needed capability.

options.text: Preserve and test the needed definitions and records while questioning how the software and routines provide them.
options.rationale: The club can retain useful knowledge without assuming every part of the old arrangement must survive.

section: The reversal, and how to reconcile it
objective: Exclude sunk spending as a sufficient reason to retain a system
stem: A distributor’s director argues against replacement because the firm spent $2 million building the current ordering system. What is the strongest basis for today’s decision?

options.text: Retain the system until future sales equal the original development bill.
options.rationale: Recovering an arbitrary historical amount does not compare the future options.

options.text: Replace it because any system that cost that much must now be inefficient.
options.rationale: Past spending alone establishes neither current usefulness nor inefficiency.

options.text: Compare future service value, support costs and the costs and risks of alternatives.
options.rationale: The prior spending is already incurred; the decision concerns what the options will provide and require from now on.

options.text: Select whichever option has the lowest equipment price.
options.rationale: Equipment price omits future service value, support, transition work and risk.

section: Nobody can buy this in the year they need it
objective: Identify accumulated knowledge that cannot be bought as equipment
stem: A new distributor buys the same ordering software used by an established competitor. It still struggles with unusual substitutions that the competitor handles confidently. Which explanation fits the chapter?

options.text: The competitor may have accumulated checked definitions, experience and trust through repeated use.
options.rationale: Matching the software does not reproduce the knowledge and routines built around it.

options.text: Identical software must produce identical business performance once installed.
options.rationale: People, records and routines can differ even when the software matches.

options.text: The competitor’s equipment must be newer because it handles exceptions better.
options.rationale: The scenario provides no evidence about equipment age; exception knowledge can explain the difference.

options.text: Unusual substitutions should be ignored because ordinary orders work.
options.rationale: Exceptions can be part of the capability customers depend on.

section: Nobody can buy this in the year they need it
objective: Choose observable evidence that knowledge is no longer held by one person
stem: Only a club’s long-serving administrator understands its unusual membership-fee exceptions. Which result would best show that a documentation project reduced this dependence?

options.text: The documentation has twice as many pages as the old notes.
options.rationale: Length does not show whether another person can apply the definitions correctly.

options.text: A second employee correctly handles representative exceptions using the checked documentation.
options.rationale: This demonstrates that the knowledge can support work beyond the original expert.

options.text: The administrator says the new file contains everything important.
options.rationale: That is useful input, but it does not demonstrate that someone else can use it.

options.text: The club buys another licence for the same membership software.
options.rationale: Access to software does not transfer understanding of the exceptions.

section: What a business graduate actually needs to know about infrastructure
objective: Interpret availability in relation to operational consequences
stem: A retailer’s supplier promises 99.9% availability measured continuously over 30 days, with no exclusions. The possible 43.2 minutes of downtime could fall just before the daily dispatch deadline. What should the manager investigate?

options.text: Whether 99.9% means that every interruption will last less than one minute.
options.rationale: The percentage does not specify how downtime is distributed into individual interruptions.

options.text: Whether the percentage guarantees downtime will occur outside ordering hours.
options.rationale: No such timing guarantee follows from a monthly percentage.

options.text: Whether all fallback arrangements can be removed because availability is above 99%.
options.rationale: A high percentage can still permit an interruption at a consequential time.

options.text: How urgent orders will be handled if the service is unavailable near the deadline.
options.rationale: The business consequence depends on when interruption occurs and what alternative work remains possible.

section: What a business graduate actually needs to know about infrastructure
objective: Distinguish high availability from uninterrupted reliability
stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes availability from reliability?

options.text: High availability means every item mapping is accurate.
options.rationale: Data accuracy is a separate issue; a service can be available while using incorrect mappings.

options.text: Availability and reliability are interchangeable measures of monthly uptime.
options.rationale: Reliability concerns performing the intended function without failure over stated conditions and time, not just access time.

options.text: A service can have high availability while frequent failures and quick restarts repeatedly interrupt work.
options.rationale: Rapid recovery can keep total downtime small even though failures are frequent.

options.text: A reliable service must be able to handle unlimited growth in demand.
options.rationale: Handling increased demand concerns scalability, and no claim of unlimited capacity follows.

section: What a business graduate actually needs to know about infrastructure
objective: Identify a non-computing constraint on scalability
stem: An events company doubles server capacity, but one manager still reviews every booking amendment. Requests pile up while the servers are mostly idle. What is the next constraint to examine?

options.text: The amendment-approval process and the manager’s capacity to perform it.
options.rationale: The arrangement’s capacity includes human work; more servers do not remove this approval bottleneck.

options.text: The server’s unused storage space as the presumed cause of the queue.
options.rationale: The scenario points to waiting for approval, not a shortage of storage.

options.text: The computing capacity used to send automatic booking confirmations.
options.rationale: The stated backlog is waiting for a person’s approval while servers are idle; it does not point to confirmation-processing capacity.

options.text: The event-booking database’s transaction speed as the presumed cause of the delay.
options.rationale: Nothing in the scenario identifies slow database operations; the visible constraint is the required human review.

section: What a business graduate actually needs to know about infrastructure
objective: Identify retained business responsibilities when subscribing to SaaS
stem: An events company subscribes to a booking application operated by a provider. Which responsibility should the company still assign internally?

options.text: Operating every server used by the provider, regardless of the agreement.
options.rationale: A provider-operated service does not automatically leave all server operation with the customer.

options.text: Deciding staff access, maintaining suitable business data and planning how booking work continues during an interruption.
options.rationale: SaaS does not transfer these business decisions and arrangements automatically to the provider.

options.text: Assuming every booking record is correct because the provider operates the application.
options.rationale: Application operation does not establish the accuracy of the company’s records.

options.text: Letting the provider set all customer refund rules without an agreed business decision.
options.rationale: Moving application operation does not by itself transfer authority over business policies.

section: The budget you actually inherit
objective: Identify a feasible project combination under a fixed annual commitment
stem: A distributor has a $200,000 annual technology budget and a fixed $140,000 operating commitment. Recovery work costs $20,000, mapping work $30,000 and a dashboard $40,000. Which plan funds two projects and leaves $10,000 uncommitted?

options.text: Recovery work and the dashboard.
options.rationale: These cost $60,000 and use the entire amount left after the operating commitment.

options.text: Mapping work and the dashboard.
options.rationale: These cost $70,000, exceeding the available $60,000.

options.text: Recovery work and mapping work.
options.rationale: The available $60,000 less $50,000 for these two projects leaves $10,000.

options.text: All three projects.
options.rationale: The three projects total $90,000, exceeding the available amount by $30,000.

section: The budget you actually inherit
objective: Use new evidence to reconsider a budget priority
stem: A distributor prioritised recovery work over a dashboard because restoration had not been demonstrated and dashboard benefits were unclear. Which new evidence would most strongly justify revisiting that priority?

options.text: The dashboard vendor offers a more fashionable visual style.
options.rationale: Appearance does not resolve the comparative business value or the recovery concern.

options.text: A director describes the dashboard as essential without identifying its effect on decisions.
options.rationale: A label is not evidence that the proposal addresses a more important need.

options.text: Recovery work is less visible to sales staff than a dashboard.
options.rationale: Visibility does not show which capability matters more to the business.

options.text: A current representative recovery test succeeds, while documented decision delays from missing sales information cause material losses.
options.rationale: This directly changes the evidence underlying both the recovery concern and the dashboard’s value.

section: The budget you actually inherit
objective: Specify a result that demonstrates capability rather than spending
stem: A club pays for a project to make its membership records recoverable. Which year-end evidence best demonstrates the intended result?

options.text: A representative restoration succeeds, and a responsible employee can follow the recovery procedure.
options.rationale: The outcome shows that usable recovery capability exists, rather than only that resources were purchased.

options.text: The supplier’s invoice is marked paid.
options.rationale: Payment proves expenditure, not that records can be restored.

options.text: The project has used the full approved budget.
options.rationale: Spending the allocation does not establish successful recovery.

options.text: The supplier has created a folder called “Recovery.”
options.rationale: A named folder does not establish that the records and procedure work.

section: The budget you actually inherit
objective: Identify continuing ownership after a one-time improvement
stem: A club has paid once to clean membership-category definitions. New categories and fee rules will be added next year. What should be settled before closing the project?

options.text: How to prohibit every future category change so the project stays complete.
options.rationale: The club may need legitimate changes; avoiding maintenance by freezing the business is not established as workable.

options.text: Who approves and checks future definition changes, and where the continuing work is budgeted.
options.rationale: Definitions can become inaccurate again unless ownership and ongoing resources are assigned.

options.text: How to record the original invoice as proof that all future definitions are checked.
options.rationale: A past payment does not verify changes made later.

options.text: Which file name will make the definitions appear permanent.
options.rationale: A name does not provide maintenance or responsibility.

section: How much protection is enough?
objective: Interpret expected loss as a probability-weighted estimate
stem: Assume a retailer estimates a 5% annual chance of a $200,000 loss and otherwise no loss from the event. What does an expected annual loss of $10,000 mean?

options.text: The retailer will lose exactly $10,000 every year.
options.rationale: Expected loss is a weighted estimate; in this simplified case the realised event loss is either zero or $200,000.

options.text: The maximum possible annual loss is $10,000.
options.rationale: The stated event can cause a $200,000 loss; the average does not cap the outcome.

options.text: The probability-weighted loss is $10,000, although an actual year can be much better or worse.
options.rationale: Five percent of $200,000 is $10,000; that estimate differs from the bill in a particular year.

options.text: After nineteen loss-free years, a $200,000 loss must occur in year twenty.
options.rationale: An annual probability does not establish a fixed calendar for the event.

section: How much protection is enough?
objective: Exclude protection options that fail a minimum service requirement
stem: A hospital requires emergency ordering during an outage. Basic protection has an estimated total annual cost of $25,000 but no emergency route. Intermediate costs $35,000 and extensive costs $48,000; both meet the requirement. On these estimates, which choice has the lowest total among feasible options?

options.text: Basic, because $25,000 is the smallest number.
options.rationale: Basic fails the stated minimum service requirement and is not a feasible choice.

options.text: Extensive, because the most expensive protection must always be best.
options.rationale: Both remaining options meet the requirement; greater cost alone does not establish a preferable choice.

options.text: Basic and a plan to decide how to order only after an outage occurs.
options.rationale: Deferring the required emergency route does not make the option meet the stated requirement.

options.text: Intermediate, because it meets the requirement at the lower estimated total.
options.rationale: Feasibility is checked first; $35,000 is lower than $48,000 among the qualifying options.

section: How much protection is enough?
objective: Test whether a protection ranking changes when loss estimates change
stem: Two hospital protection options meet minimum requirements. Intermediate costs $20,000 plus $15,000 expected annual loss; extensive costs $40,000 plus $8,000 expected loss. New evidence raises intermediate’s expected loss to $35,000, leaving other estimates unchanged. What follows from the revised estimates?

options.text: Extensive now has the lower total: $48,000 versus $55,000.
options.rationale: Intermediate’s revised total is $20,000 + $35,000; extensive remains $40,000 + $8,000.

options.text: Intermediate remains cheaper because its protection price has not changed.
options.rationale: Protection price alone omits the revised expected loss.

options.text: The options are tied because both meet the same minimum requirements.
options.rationale: Meeting the requirements establishes feasibility, not equal cost.

options.text: No comparison is possible because expected losses are estimates.
options.rationale: Uncertainty requires examination, but estimates can still support a conditional comparison.

section: How much protection is enough?
objective: Avoid judging a precaution solely by the absence of a realised failure
stem: A retailer completes a year without the outage its protection plan was designed for. A manager calls the entire expenditure waste. What is the strongest response?

options.text: A loss-free year proves the protection eliminated every possible future outage.
options.rationale: A single outcome does not establish that all future risk has disappeared.

options.text: Review the evidence available when the decision was made, protection delivered and new information before judging or changing it.
options.rationale: The realised year alone does not show whether the precaution was justified before the outcome was known.

options.text: Keep the same spending forever because precautions cannot be evaluated.
options.rationale: Protection should be reviewed as evidence and requirements change.

options.text: Cancel protection until an outage proves that the business needs it.
options.rationale: This treats a loss-free outcome as proof of no risk and waits for harm rather than evaluating the decision.

section: Your turn
objective: Test whether an exported file makes a switch operationally usable
stem: A membership vendor offers a spreadsheet export containing unexplained category codes. The club calls this a complete exit plan. What small test would best challenge that claim?

options.text: Confirm that the file size is larger than last year’s export.
options.rationale: Size does not establish that the records can be interpreted and used elsewhere.

options.text: Confirm that the file can be emailed to a replacement vendor.
options.rationale: Transferring bytes does not establish that the receiving party understands their meaning.

options.text: Transfer a sample, interpret its codes and check that another person or system can use the records correctly.
options.rationale: A usable exit requires understood definitions and verified use, not merely possession of a file.

options.text: Print the file and store it without checking the fields.
options.rationale: A paper copy retains unexplained codes rather than resolving their meaning.

section: Your turn
objective: Choose early learning that builds capability before a future need is certain
stem: A growing club may need more complex membership arrangements next year, but the exact requirements are unknown. Which action now most directly builds useful capability?

options.text: Buy the largest software package before identifying recurring exceptions.
options.rationale: A larger tool does not establish which knowledge and arrangements the club will need.

options.text: Wait until growth occurs before recording how current exceptions are resolved.
options.rationale: This loses an opportunity to accumulate and share knowledge through current work.

options.text: Keep exception decisions private so only the experienced administrator can make them.
options.rationale: Concentrating knowledge increases dependence rather than building a shared capability.

options.text: Keep a checked history of recurring exceptions and the reasons for their resolution, then use it to identify future requirements.
options.rationale: Experience can accumulate as usable knowledge before the club knows the exact future design; it need not commit now to a large purchase.

section: What counts as a hit?
objective: Identify a useful contribution excluded by a familiar measure
stem: A baseball team values batters mainly by batting average, which excludes walks. Its aim is to acquire affordable players who help it score runs. What should the team investigate?

options.text: Whether players with the highest batting average are automatically the cheapest.
options.rationale: The measure alone establishes neither price nor affordability.

options.text: Whether contributions such as reaching base through walks are useful but underpriced.
options.rationale: A familiar measure can omit a contribution that matters to the outcome and to purchasing value.

options.text: Whether excluding walks makes all batting-average calculations mathematically incorrect.
options.rationale: The definition can be applied correctly while omitting something relevant to the decision.

options.text: Whether every player with many walks must be a better purchase than every other player.
options.rationale: One contribution alone does not settle the player’s overall value or price.

section: What counts as a hit?
objective: Distinguish the loss of a pricing advantage from the loss of usefulness of analysis
stem: Teams increasingly recognise and pay for contributions that an early analyst found underpriced. What follows about the analyst’s approach?

options.text: The original contribution no longer helps a team score once rivals value it.
options.rationale: A market price correction does not remove the contribution’s sporting usefulness.

options.text: The original underpricing must have been imaginary because it later disappeared.
options.rationale: A temporary advantage can be real before competitors learn and prices adjust.

options.text: Teams should stop examining what their measures omit because the first insight has spread.
options.rationale: The spread of one insight does not remove the value of asking better questions.

options.text: The specific pricing advantage may shrink while the ability to evaluate contributions remains useful.
options.rationale: Rivals’ learning can change capture of value without making analytical capability worthless.

section: Three answers to one question
objective: Identify the entity represented by a row before interpreting its count
stem: A data view contains one row per subscription. What does counting its rows directly establish?

options.text: The number of subscription records in that view.
options.rationale: The row count follows the view’s stated unit; it does not automatically count people or billing accounts.

options.text: The number of distinct people, even when a person has several subscriptions.
options.rationale: One person can appear in several subscription rows.

options.text: The number of billing accounts, even when an account contains several subscriptions.
options.rationale: Several rows may belong to one account.

options.text: The number of paying customers regardless of the view’s fields.
options.rationale: Subscription records alone do not establish a chosen customer definition or payment status.

section: Three answers to one question
objective: Count distinct qualifying people when one person appears in multiple records
stem: Four subscription rows show: P01/S100/Active Yes; P01/S101/Active Yes; P02/S102/Active No; P03/S103/Active Yes. Active has the same definition and reporting period in every row. How many distinct people have activity on at least one subscription?

options.text: Three, because three rows say Yes.
options.rationale: This counts P01 twice and therefore counts active subscriptions rather than active people.

options.text: Four, because there are four subscription records.
options.rationale: The row total includes an inactive row and multiple records for P01.

options.text: Two: P01 and P03.
options.rationale: Both qualify, and P01 is counted once despite having two active subscriptions.

options.text: One, because only P01 has more than one active subscription.
options.rationale: The condition is activity on at least one subscription, not on more than one.

section: Three answers to one question
objective: Avoid deleting valid related records when counting people
stem: An event file has two rows for attendee E07: one for a morning workshop and one for an afternoon workshop. An analyst wants the number of attendees. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Delete the afternoon booking because E07 appears twice.
options.rationale: The second row records a different legitimate booking; deleting it would lose information.

options.text: Count E07 once for attendance while retaining both workshop records.
options.rationale: Removing duplicate counting is different from removing valid records for distinct activities.

options.text: Count E07 as two people because both bookings are valid.
options.rationale: Two valid bookings do not make two distinct attendees.

options.text: Exclude E07 entirely until the attendee selects only one workshop.
options.rationale: No inconsistency is established by a person attending different workshops.

section: Three answers to one question
objective: Explain disagreement caused by dashboard refresh timing
stem: A billing account was corrected at noon. The operational system shows the correction, but a dashboard refreshed overnight still shows the old count. What should the manager check first?

options.text: Whether the correction should be reversed to match the dashboard.
options.rationale: An older display is not a reason to reverse a valid operational correction.

options.text: Whether a dashboard count is always more authoritative than a source record.
options.rationale: A polished display may use older selected results rather than live records.

options.text: Whether the two counts can be averaged to obtain the current count.
options.rationale: Averaging different reporting times does not establish the current state.

options.text: The source and refresh time of the dashboard before interpreting the discrepancy.
options.rationale: A delayed refresh can explain the difference without an error in the correction itself.

section: Which number belongs in the presentation?
objective: Identify why an accumulated contact count is insufficient for staffing
stem: A support director wants next month’s staffing plan. A report supplies the number of people who have ever contacted support. What further evidence is most relevant?

options.text: Recent request volumes, handling work, arrival patterns and expected changes in demand.
options.rationale: Staffing depends on prospective workload and timing, not just the accumulated number of past users.

options.text: The active-person count, assuming each active person will submit one request next month.
options.rationale: Active use does not establish a support request or the work and timing that such requests would require.

options.text: The number of billing accounts ever created, without contact information.
options.rationale: Another accumulated entity count still does not describe the coming workload.

options.text: The lifetime contact-person count divided by twelve as a monthly staffing estimate.
options.rationale: Dividing an accumulated person count by twelve does not establish next month’s request volume, handling work or arrival pattern.

section: Which number belongs in the presentation?
objective: Label a measure with an entity, condition and period
stem: A report counts each person once if any of their subscriptions had recorded use in the twelve months ending 31 August 2026. Which label most accurately communicates that result?

options.text: Total subscriptions at 31 August 2026.
options.rationale: The calculation counts people with activity, not all subscription records.

options.text: Paying customers in August 2026.
options.rationale: The calculation does not test payment and uses twelve months rather than one month.

options.text: Distinct people with recorded subscription use in the twelve months ending 31 August 2026.
options.rationale: The label states the entity, qualifying condition and reporting period used.

options.text: All people who have ever used the service.
options.rationale: The lifetime population is broader than the stated twelve-month window.

section: Which number belongs in the presentation?
objective: Separate a definition change from a change in business activity
stem: A dashboard changes “active customer” from any recorded use to paid use. The next count is lower, and the director calls it a loss of customer engagement. What must be established first?

options.text: Whether the smaller count makes the new definition unacceptable in every context.
options.rationale: A narrower definition may be useful for some decisions; usefulness depends on purpose.

options.text: Whether the decline remains when periods are compared using a consistent definition.
options.rationale: A change in the qualifying rule can create a decline without any change in behaviour.

options.text: Whether the previous count should be erased so only one definition is visible.
options.rationale: Erasing the earlier basis conceals the comparability problem rather than explaining it.

options.text: Whether the difference can be treated as unpaid invoices without checking payment records.
options.rationale: The difference in active-person definitions does not by itself count unpaid invoices.

section: A precise answer to the wrong question
objective: Investigate identity before merging apparent duplicates
stem: An event database contains two attendee IDs with the same name. An analyst proposes merging them automatically. What is the strongest reason to check further?

options.text: Different people can share a name, so additional evidence is needed to establish whether the IDs represent one person.
options.rationale: A name match alone does not establish identity and can lead to an incorrect merge.

options.text: Different IDs always prove that two different people exist.
options.rationale: A single person may have registered twice under different identifiers.

options.text: Identical names always prove that one record is an error.
options.rationale: Shared names are possible, and both records may be valid.

options.text: Merging records is harmless as long as the final count is smaller.
options.rationale: A smaller count can still be wrong and may combine different people’s information.

section: A precise answer to the wrong question
objective: Distinguish accurate activity data from evidence of payment
stem: Every activity record in a subscription file is correct. The director asks how many people paid for the service, and an analyst offers the active-person count. What is the problem?

options.text: Accurate records cannot be used in a report that asks a different question.
options.rationale: They may contribute useful context, but their accuracy does not make the offered count answer the payment question.

options.text: The count must be arithmetically wrong because the director asked about payment.
options.rationale: The activity calculation may be correct under its own definition.

options.text: The director must redefine paying customers to mean active people.
options.rationale: The measure should fit the intended decision rather than changing the question to fit available data.

options.text: Recorded use does not establish payment, so accurate data can still answer the wrong question.
options.rationale: Data accuracy and suitability of a measure are separate requirements.

section: A precise answer to the wrong question
objective: Preserve uncertainty when interpreting missing values
stem: An event file has Yes, No and blank values for “attended a workshop.” Some older records predate collection of that field. How should an analyst treat the blanks?

options.text: Convert every blank to No because no attendance was recorded.
options.rationale: Absence of a collected value is not evidence that the person did not attend.

options.text: Convert every blank to Yes because older attendees probably joined a workshop.
options.rationale: That fills missing evidence with an unsupported assumption.

options.text: Investigate their meaning and distinguish missing information from a recorded No.
options.rationale: Older records may lack the field entirely, so the uncertainty should remain visible.

options.text: Remove all older attendees from every organisational report.
options.rationale: This would discard potentially useful records without regard to each report’s purpose.

section: A precise answer to the wrong question
objective: Check whether changed event capture produced apparent growth
stem: A new app begins recording mobile use that the prior system missed. Reported active people rise sharply after release. Which check best separates behavioural growth from improved observation?

options.text: Treat the increase as confirmed engagement growth because the app records it automatically.
options.rationale: Automatic recording does not establish comparability with the old capture process.

options.text: Examine known cases under both capture methods, explain the break and assess whether earlier periods can be recalculated.
options.rationale: This investigates what became observable and whether comparable historical counts can be produced.

options.text: Keep the old and new counts on one trend line without noting the release.
options.rationale: That conceals the change in what the measure can observe.

options.text: Assume the new count is wrong because it is higher than the old one.
options.rationale: The new capture may be more complete; a difference does not prove error.

section: The measure becomes the target
objective: State the warning about turning a measure into a target
stem: What warning does the chapter associate with Goodhart’s law?

options.text: Every numerical target inevitably makes performance worse.
options.rationale: The chapter treats it as a warning about incentives, not a universal prediction of failure.

options.text: A computer-generated measure cannot be influenced by employee behaviour.
options.rationale: The computer may record actions accurately while people change which actions they perform.

options.text: Managers should replace all measures with personal impressions.
options.rationale: The warning calls for better interpretation and checks, not abandonment of measurement.

options.text: Using a measure as a target can change behaviour and weaken its connection to the intended outcome.
options.rationale: Rewards or penalties can encourage activity that improves the measure without improving the result.

section: The measure becomes the target
objective: Calculate an outcome warning alongside a rising activity target
stem: A team closes 80 tickets in period A and 100 in period B. Of those tickets, eight from A and 25 from B reopen within the same follow-up window. Which comparison is correct?

options.text: Closures rose, while the reopening rate rose from 10% to 25%.
options.rationale: Eight divided by 80 is 10%; 25 divided by 100 is 25%. More closures coincide with a stronger warning about unresolved work.

options.text: Closures rose, while the reopening rate fell from 25% to 10%.
options.rationale: This reverses the two rates.

options.text: Reopening was 8% in A and 25% in B.
options.rationale: The first rate uses 80 closed tickets as its denominator, not 100.

options.text: Both periods had the same reopening rate because the follow-up window was equal.
options.rationale: Equal follow-up makes the rates more comparable; it does not make the outcomes identical.

section: The measure becomes the target
objective: Identify behaviour that improves a target while leaving important work unresolved
stem: A warehouse rewards staff only for the number of orders dispatched. Difficult orders begin waiting much longer while staff select easy orders first. What should the manager recognise?

options.text: The higher dispatch count proves every customer is receiving better service.
options.rationale: An aggregate activity count can hide worsening service for the orders left behind.

options.text: The dispatch records must be false if difficult orders still wait.
options.rationale: The records can be accurate while the incentive changes the mix of work selected.

options.text: The target can encourage selection of easy work while the age of unresolved orders worsens.
options.rationale: Improving a count can diverge from completing the work customers need.

options.text: Difficult orders should be removed from the service definition because they lower productivity.
options.rationale: Changing the definition to exclude hard cases conceals the unmet need rather than resolving it.

section: The measure becomes the target
objective: Choose investigation instead of treating a target shift as proof of misconduct
stem: After a dispatch bonus begins, a warehouse records more shipments and more returns. A product change occurred at the same time. What is the best next step?

options.text: Conclude that the bonus caused careless work and discipline the team.
options.rationale: The timing alone does not separate incentive effects from product or other changes.

options.text: Review returned orders with staff, distinguish error types and compare affected products before deciding what to change.
options.rationale: This gathers evidence about the mechanism rather than assigning a cause from coincident trends.

options.text: Ignore returns because the rewarded measure improved.
options.rationale: Returns may reveal a deterioration in the desired outcome that the headline count misses.

options.text: Add a separate target for every recorded field without examining returned orders.
options.rationale: More targets do not identify the cause and can make the desired result harder to see.

section: When the spreadsheet and the experienced manager disagree
objective: Distinguish elapsed resolution time from active work time
stem: A support case requires 20 minutes of agent work but remains open for two days while the customer supplies information. A report labels two days as agent work time. What needs correction?

options.text: The case should be removed because any customer waiting makes it unmeasurable.
options.rationale: Both elapsed and active work can be measured if they are defined appropriately.

options.text: The 20 minutes should be replaced with two days in all staffing calculations.
options.rationale: This treats waiting time as labour time and can misstate workload.

options.text: The customer’s delay proves the agent worked inefficiently.
options.rationale: The waiting period alone does not establish inefficient active work.

options.text: The report must distinguish elapsed time to resolution from time actively spent working.
options.rationale: The two measures answer different questions about customer experience and staffing.

section: When the spreadsheet and the experienced manager disagree
objective: Calculate how case mix changes an overall average without a pace difference
stem: For either team, simple claim reviews take 10 minutes of work and complex reviews take 40. Team A handles six simple and four complex cases; Team B handles nine simple and one complex case. There are no transfers or waits. What do the averages show?

options.text: A averages 22 minutes and B 13, although their pace on each type is identical.
options.rationale: A uses 60 + 160 = 220 minutes for ten cases; B uses 90 + 40 = 130. The mix explains the overall difference.

options.text: A averages 22 minutes and B 13, proving A is slower on comparable work.
options.rationale: The averages are correct, but the stated within-type times are identical.

options.text: Both average 25 minutes because 10 and 40 average to 25.
options.rationale: That unweighted mean ignores the different numbers of each case type.

options.text: A averages 13 minutes and B 22 because simple cases dominate A’s work.
options.rationale: This reverses the workloads and calculated averages.

section: When the spreadsheet and the experienced manager disagree
objective: Test an experienced supervisor’s explanation with comparable groups
stem: A claims supervisor says her team’s longer average reflects more complex cases and transferred files. Which analysis would best test that explanation?

options.text: Compare the same overall averages again to more decimal places.
options.rationale: More precision does not control for case type or transfers.

options.text: Accept the explanation because the supervisor has the longest service.
options.rationale: Experience can suggest a mechanism, but the explanation still needs evidence.

options.text: Separate comparable case types, identify transfers and compare team performance within those groups.
options.rationale: This tests whether the difference is associated with the mix and movement of work.

options.text: Compare team sizes without examining the work each team receives.
options.rationale: Staff numbers alone do not establish case complexity or the handling of transferred time.

section: When the spreadsheet and the experienced manager disagree
objective: Choose a provisional action with a defined learning condition
stem: A support manager must act this week on a disputed evening-team average. A full study will take longer, and no urgent safety issue is identified. Which response best follows the chapter?

options.text: Impose a permanent penalty now because a higher average is sufficient evidence.
options.rationale: The average may reflect case mix or conditions rather than individual performance.

options.text: Defer a punitive decision, inspect a small sample and test added specialist coverage with a stated continuation criterion.
options.rationale: This makes a bounded action depend on evidence while acknowledging the remaining uncertainty.

options.text: Stop collecting evidence because the deadline makes analysis irrelevant.
options.rationale: A small relevant check can still improve the immediate decision.

options.text: Collect another month of the same overall average without defining what it should resolve.
options.rationale: More of the same measure may not distinguish the competing explanations.

section: Three debts, briefly paid
objective: Distinguish disagreement about decision criteria from disagreement about records
stem: Two buyers agree on a company’s system records and performance. One values continuity; the other needs easy integration with its own systems. They reach different valuations. What should an analyst examine first?

options.text: Which buyer must have made an arithmetic error because the records agree.
options.rationale: Shared records do not require identical valuations when objectives differ.

options.text: How to force both buyers to use continuity as their only criterion.
options.rationale: That would ignore the second buyer’s stated purpose for the acquisition.

options.text: Which dataset should be deleted to eliminate the disagreement.
options.rationale: The disagreement is not identified as a conflict in records.

options.text: How each buyer’s purpose changes the criteria used to judge the same facts.
options.rationale: Different objectives can support different evaluations; the criteria should be made explicit and examined.

section: Three debts, briefly paid
objective: Treat a stated assumption as a claim still requiring support
stem: An analyst assumes that every billing account represents exactly two people and doubles the account count to estimate people served. The assumption is disclosed beside the estimate. What does that disclosure achieve?

options.text: It makes the assumption visible for challenge, but does not establish that it is true.
options.rationale: An explicit assumption can be assessed; evidence about people per account is still needed to support this conversion.

options.text: It converts the estimate into a verified count of distinct people.
options.rationale: A label does not establish how many people each account represents.

options.text: It makes the estimate equally defensible to a count based on checked person records.
options.rationale: Different evidential support still matters after assumptions are disclosed.

options.text: It eliminates the need to assess whether the estimate fits the director’s decision.
options.rationale: A disclosed assumption may still be unsuitable for the decision being made.

section: Optional: what a price tells you
objective: Interpret excess implied probability without treating it as guaranteed profit
stem: Optional odds item. Two fictional prices imply break-even probabilities of 60% and 43.48%, for a total of 103.48%. Which interpretation follows?

options.text: Every accepted wager guarantees a 3.48% profit to the seller.
options.rationale: Realised profit depends on the stakes accepted and the outcome, among other things; the excess is not such a guarantee.

options.text: The two outcomes together have a true probability of 103.48%.
options.rationale: Mutually exclusive, exhaustive outcomes have probabilities totalling 100%; these price-derived figures are not directly such a pair.

options.text: The overround is 103.48%, exceeding 100% by 3.48 percentage points.
options.rationale: This describes the sum of the price-derived break-even probabilities without claiming it reveals true chances or realised profit.

options.text: The excess proves one outcome’s true probability must be reduced by exactly 3.48 points.
options.rationale: The arithmetic alone does not identify how pricing excess is distributed between outcomes.

section: Optional: what a price tells you
objective: Distinguish mathematical normalisation from evidence of true chances
stem: Optional odds item. An analyst divides each price-derived implied probability by their sum, producing values that add to 100%. What has this established?

options.text: The true chances have been discovered because the total now equals 100%.
options.rationale: A consistent total does not validate the assumption used to remove the pricing excess.

options.text: A consistent pair under proportional adjustment, not proof of the true chances.
options.rationale: The normalisation removes the excess proportionally; that assumption needs justification beyond the arithmetic.

options.text: The seller’s realised profit is zero because no probability excess remains in the adjusted figures.
options.rationale: Changing the presentation of the numbers does not change actual prices, stakes or outcomes.

options.text: The original prices contain no information about expectations.
options.rationale: The limitation of normalisation does not establish that prices are wholly uninformative.

section: Your turn
objective: Track which entity counts change when a person adds an account and subscription
stem: A file has three distinct people, two billing accounts and four subscriptions; P02 is already an active person. A new row adds P02’s active subscription S104 under a new account A30. Which counts increase?

options.text: People, accounts, subscriptions and active people all increase by one.
options.rationale: P02 was already counted as a person and as active; those two totals do not increase.

options.text: Only active people increase, because the new row says Active Yes.
options.rationale: The person was already active, while the account and subscription are new.

options.text: Only subscriptions increase, because an existing person cannot have a new account.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly adds a distinct billing account for the existing person.

options.text: Accounts and subscriptions each increase by one; people and active people stay unchanged.
options.rationale: The row adds two new entities but no new person or newly qualifying active person.

section: What the internet is made of
objective: Distinguish a wireless access link from the complete internet journey
stem: What does “wireless” establish about a device’s internet connection?

options.text: The entire route to every remote service avoids cables.
options.rationale: A wireless first link can connect to networks that use terrestrial and undersea cables.

options.text: A link uses wireless communication; the rest of the journey can depend on cables and other equipment.
options.rationale: Wireless describes a link, not every part of the route between the device and a service.

options.text: The remote application runs on the device rather than in a building elsewhere.
options.rationale: Wireless access does not determine where an application is hosted.

options.text: The device has an independent alternative to every upstream failure.
options.rationale: A wireless link can share upstream dependencies with other paths.

section: What the internet is made of
objective: Identify physical responsibilities that remain when a service moves to the cloud
stem: A warehouse moves its inventory application to a cloud provider. A manager says power and building failures no longer concern the service because it is online. What is the best correction?

options.text: Cloud applications cannot depend on the warehouse’s local equipment.
options.rationale: Staff still need a usable way to reach and use the application.

options.text: The warehouse must now personally operate every provider building.
options.rationale: The supplier may operate the infrastructure; dependence does not imply direct operation by the customer.

options.text: A cloud contract guarantees that physical infrastructure cannot fail.
options.rationale: A contract does not make equipment, power and connections cease to matter.

options.text: The provider still operates physical computers, power and connections on which the service depends.
options.rationale: Responsibility may move to a supplier, but the underlying physical dependencies remain.

section: What the internet is made of
objective: Identify conditions needed for an alternative physical route to help
stem: A warehouse learns that a second cable exists in the region. Its manager treats this as proof that overseas inventory access can survive damage to the current cable. What is still needed?

options.text: Evidence that a working alternative can carry the warehouse’s traffic with adequate capacity and reach the service.
options.rationale: A cable’s existence does not establish that it is an available, sufficient route for this traffic.

options.text: A photograph showing the second cable’s protective covering.
options.rationale: A photograph does not establish reachability, operational status or available capacity.

options.text: A count of every cable in other oceans.
options.rationale: A global count does not show which alternative this warehouse can actually use.

options.text: Confirmation that the inventory application has a modern interface.
options.rationale: The interface does not establish a usable physical route.

section: The dependency you never agreed to
objective: Distinguish a network connection from an unavailable destination service
stem: A shop can browse websites through its backup connection, but its payment provider confirms that the payment service itself is unavailable. Why can sales still fail?

options.text: Opening any website proves the payment terminal must be defective.
options.rationale: A working website establishes neither terminal failure nor availability of a different service.

options.text: A faster backup connection will necessarily restore the provider’s service.
options.rationale: Connection speed does not repair an unavailable destination service.

options.text: Working internet access does not make the separate payment service available.
options.rationale: The business transaction depends on both transport and the service that processes it.

options.text: The shop should assume payments succeeded because the internet connection works.
options.rationale: Network access alone is not evidence that a payment was processed.

section: The dependency you never agreed to
objective: Distinguish redundancy from diversity for a specified failure
stem: Which statement best distinguishes redundancy from diversity?

options.text: Redundancy means two supplier names; diversity means two bills.
options.rationale: Names and invoices do not establish how paths or failures differ.

options.text: Redundancy adds a component or path; diversity avoids sharing the particular failure being addressed.
options.rationale: An additional route can remain exposed to the same failure unless relevant dependencies differ.

options.text: Redundancy prevents local failures; diversity guarantees protection from every regional failure.
options.rationale: Neither term provides a universal guarantee across all failure conditions.

options.text: Diversity means the backup has a higher speed than the primary connection.
options.rationale: Speed and failure independence are different properties.

section: Follow one payment
objective: Recognise a shared physical route despite different suppliers
stem: A shop buys fixed connections from two providers. Both enter the building through the same duct. What does this imply about protection against that duct being severed?

options.text: Two contracts guarantee that one line survives any physical cut.
options.rationale: Contract count does not separate the cables’ physical exposure.

options.text: Only the cheaper connection can be damaged because it is the backup.
options.rationale: Price and designation do not determine whether the shared duct is affected.

options.text: The connections provide no benefit against any conceivable failure.
options.rationale: They may help with some faults, even though the shared duct remains a common dependency.

options.text: Both connections may fail together, so the second does not avoid that specific failure.
options.rationale: The relevant physical exposure is shared despite different provider names.

section: Follow one payment
objective: Identify a local dependency that an upstream alternative cannot bypass
