stem: A warehouse has two independent upstream carriers, but both connections use one local router. That router stops working. Which issue should the continuity plan address?

options.text: How the warehouse will bypass or replace the failed local router.
options.rationale: Neither upstream route helps if traffic cannot leave through the shared failed local equipment.

options.text: How to buy more capacity from both carriers while retaining the failed router.
options.rationale: More upstream capacity does not restore the local path.

options.text: How to switch to the other carrier using the same failed router.
options.rationale: The local failure remains on that route.

options.text: How to demand that the inventory provider change its application interface.
options.rationale: An interface change does not repair the stated network equipment failure.

section: Follow one payment
objective: Handle a payment request whose result is uncertain
stem: A shop sends a payment request, but the connection drops before confirmation arrives. Which instruction should staff follow?

options.text: Repeat it immediately as a new sale because no confirmation proves rejection.
options.rationale: The original request may have succeeded; a new request could duplicate the transaction.

options.text: Mark the sale paid because the terminal transmitted a request.
options.rationale: Transmission does not establish successful processing and confirmation.

options.text: Use the payment supplier’s approved procedure to establish status before deciding whether to retry.
options.rationale: The result is uncertain, so the procedure must distinguish a completed payment from one needing another attempt.

options.text: Erase the local sale record so the reconnection starts cleanly.
options.rationale: Removing evidence makes it harder to establish and reconcile what occurred.

section: Buying a backup that answers the question
objective: Choose the backup supported by evidence for the stated failure
stem: A shop wants protection from a local fixed-line cut. A second fixed line shares the same duct. A separately operated mobile route has verified coverage, capacity and a different upstream path. What is the best-supported choice for this risk?

options.text: The second fixed line, because fixed lines are always more dependable than mobile links.
options.rationale: That general claim ignores the shared duct exposed to the specified cut.

options.text: The tested mobile route, while retaining the dependencies and limits that remain.
options.rationale: The route evidence supports avoiding this fixed-line failure, not every possible outage.

options.text: Either option, because both add a second connection.
options.rationale: The two alternatives differ in their exposure to the specified failure.

options.text: The mobile route as proof that all payment-service outages are now covered.
options.rationale: A different route still relies on the destination service and other infrastructure.

section: Buying a backup that answers the question
objective: Make switchover operationally available to staff
stem: A shop’s backup works when the owner changes a setting, but only the owner has access and is usually absent on Saturdays. What should be settled before calling the backup ready?

options.text: Whether the equipment can be labelled as automatic backup in the inventory.
options.rationale: A label cannot make the manual action available during an interruption.

options.text: Whether the owner can explain the password after returning on Monday.
options.rationale: That does not preserve Saturday’s work.

options.text: Whether the shop can buy a faster version of the same primary line.
options.rationale: Primary speed does not address who can activate the existing backup.

options.text: Which authorised on-duty employee can switch, with the access and instructions needed.
options.rationale: A workable backup includes available people and authority, not only a functioning technical path.

section: Buying a backup that answers the question
objective: Choose a controlled test of the intended business action
stem: A warehouse has installed a backup route for dispatch confirmation. Which test best establishes whether authorised staff can use it?

options.text: Arrange a controlled primary-path interruption with supplier support, complete an approved test confirmation and test the return to normal.
options.rationale: This checks the intended business action and the switch in both directions under agreed conditions.

options.text: Open a public web page on the backup and treat dispatch confirmation as established.
options.rationale: A web page does not test the dispatch service or its required workflow.

options.text: Disconnect equipment during peak live dispatch without telling the operations team.
options.rationale: Uncontrolled disruption creates avoidable operational risk and is not the proposed testing approach.

options.text: Accept the installation invoice as evidence that every required action works.
options.rationale: Payment for installation does not demonstrate the operational outcome.

section: Buying a backup that answers the question
objective: Limit a test conclusion to the conditions actually exercised
stem: An authorised test bypasses a warehouse’s primary access line and successfully confirms a dispatch. Both routes still use the same regional carrier. What does the test establish?

options.text: The warehouse has survived a simulated failure of the shared regional carrier.
options.rationale: The regional carrier was not the failure bypassed in this test.

options.text: Every dispatch service outage can now be handled automatically.
options.rationale: One successful route test cannot establish every failure mode or switching behaviour.

options.text: The tested access-line failure was handled under those conditions; regional-carrier failure remains untested and shared.
options.rationale: A narrow success should be recorded without extending it to a different common dependency.

options.text: The successful result is irrelevant because the design is not independent of every failure.
options.rationale: It provides useful evidence for the tested failure even though protection is limited.

section: Buying a backup that answers the question
objective: Prioritise essential traffic when backup capacity is limited
stem: A shop’s backup handles a test payment when empty. During an outage, customer Wi-Fi and large stock downloads consume most of its capacity. Which response best supports continuity?

options.text: Treat the earlier single-payment test as proof that peak usage needs no further attention.
options.rationale: The test did not establish performance under the competing workload now described.

options.text: Reserve capacity for payments and essential communication, defer large updates and test the essential workload.
options.rationale: The business must choose which work to preserve and check that the backup supports it at an acceptable pace.

options.text: Give all traffic equal priority regardless of its role in completing sales.
options.rationale: Equal treatment can leave essential work competing with deferrable activity.

options.text: Remove all transaction-status checks to make payments use fewer messages.
options.rationale: Dropping business checks can create uncertainty and record errors rather than a sound capacity solution.

section: Keep some business moving
objective: Choose a fallback that does not presume an unconfirmed card payment is authorised
stem: A shop’s payment service is down through every available connection. Its provider has not approved offline card processing. Which fallback is consistent with the chapter?

options.text: Collect card details on improvised paper forms for later processing.
options.rationale: An outage is not the time to invent an unsupported procedure for handling card details.

options.text: Treat every transmitted card request as authorised and hand over goods.
options.rationale: Transmission without a confirmed result does not establish authorisation.

options.text: Promise customers that offline card processing must work because the terminal has a battery.
options.rationale: Power does not establish a provider-supported payment function.

options.text: Use agreed cash-handling arrangements or reserve goods for later completion, explaining the limits to customers.
options.rationale: These can preserve some work without claiming an unconfirmed card transaction succeeded.

section: Keep some business moving
objective: Plan reconciliation of deferred work and business records
stem: During an inventory-service outage, a warehouse records permitted reservations on a controlled list. Service returns. What is the key next step?

options.text: Assign someone to reconcile reservations, completed orders and stock before treating the records as normal.
options.rationale: Recovery must establish what actually occurred so work is neither lost nor duplicated.

options.text: Delete the list immediately because the online inventory is now reachable.
options.rationale: Reachability does not incorporate the work recorded during the interruption.

options.text: Enter every reservation as a completed shipment without checking its status.
options.rationale: A reservation is not necessarily a shipment; automatic conversion could create false stock movements.

options.text: Leave both record sets indefinitely without assigning a person to compare them.
options.rationale: Parallel unexamined records retain uncertainty about the current business position.

section: Keep some business moving
objective: Turn a technical fallback into instructions staff can act on
stem: A warehouse’s outage folder lists routers and supplier phone numbers but gives no operating instructions. What should a short fallback procedure add?

options.text: A longer description of every device’s manufacturing history.
options.rationale: Equipment background does not tell staff which work to continue or stop.

options.text: A statement that every employee should improvise according to personal judgement.
options.rationale: Uncoordinated actions can produce inconsistent decisions and records.

options.text: Who declares the interruption, what work may continue, what must be recorded and when staff should stop.
options.rationale: These decisions make the fallback usable by the people carrying out the work.

options.text: A promise that no sales or dispatches will ever be lost.
options.rationale: A promise does not define actions and may exceed what a limited fallback can preserve.

section: The satellites, and what they change
objective: Distinguish a functioning network from a viable original investment
stem: A fictional satellite network works technically but its original venture fails financially. New owners buy the assets cheaply and operate successfully. What can a manager conclude about the original investment?

options.text: The later success proves the original construction cost was economically justified.
options.rationale: Later owners may face a different cost base, so their success does not validate the original investment.

options.text: Technical usefulness and later commercial success do not by themselves establish that the original cost and business model were viable.
options.rationale: The equipment can work while the economics differ between the original venture and its successor.

options.text: The original financial failure proves the network could never provide a useful service.
options.rationale: Financial failure and technical usefulness are distinct claims.

options.text: The only explanation must be that the idea arrived a fixed number of years too early.
options.rationale: The scenario does not isolate timing from financing, customers, prices or operating arrangements.

section: The satellites, and what they change
objective: Reject a single-cause explanation drawn from unlike satellite businesses
stem: A presenter compares an old satellite-phone venture with a newer satellite-broadband service and credits the newer outcome entirely to cheaper launch costs. Which response best follows the chapter?

options.text: Accept the explanation because both businesses use satellites.
options.rationale: Shared technology does not make their markets, equipment and operating arrangements equivalent.

options.text: Reject any possible relevance of launch costs because the services differ.
options.rationale: Costs may matter, but the comparison does not establish their isolated effect.

options.text: Compare only the number of satellites and ignore the customers served.
options.rationale: A component count does not control for the differences in service and economics.

options.text: Examine differences in customers, equipment, financing and service before attributing the outcome to one cost change.
options.rationale: The comparison involves several changing conditions and cannot isolate one cause by itself.

section: The satellites, and what they change
objective: Specify site conditions needed for a proposed satellite backup
stem: A remote shop is offered satellite broadband as a backup. What should the owner establish before relying on it?

options.text: Required equipment, usable sky view, power and enough capacity to reach the shop’s application.
options.rationale: A satellite path still requires installed, powered equipment and usable end-to-end performance.

options.text: Only whether the service is advertised as newer than the fixed connection.
options.rationale: Novelty does not establish practical suitability at the site.

options.text: Only whether the satellite is closer to Earth than another system’s satellite.
options.rationale: Orbit alone does not settle installation, power, service access or capacity.

options.text: Whether the backup eliminates the need to power local devices.
options.rationale: A different external route does not remove the devices’ power requirement.

section: The satellites, and what they change
objective: Evaluate an alternative by the work it preserves rather than its novelty
stem: A remote shop cannot obtain a second terrestrial route. A tested satellite service can support urgent ordering during local cable repairs, but costs more than the primary line. What comparison is most useful?

options.text: Select it automatically because newer infrastructure must be preferable.
options.rationale: The date or novelty of a technology does not establish that its benefit justifies its cost.

options.text: Reject it automatically because a backup should always cost less than the primary service.
options.rationale: A higher-cost alternative may still justify itself by preserving important work.

options.text: Compare the cost with the value of urgent work it preserves and the limits of other feasible fallbacks.
options.rationale: The decision concerns useful continuity for plausible failures, given available alternatives.

options.text: Assume it is worthwhile only if satellites eventually replace all terrestrial cables.
options.rationale: The local continuity decision does not require a global replacement forecast.

section: Who owns the middle, again
objective: Evaluate supplier concentration as both capability and common exposure
stem: A retailer receives strong support from several resellers, but all depend on one upstream provider. What should its continuity assessment recognise?

options.text: Good reseller support proves an upstream outage cannot affect the retailer.
options.rationale: Support quality does not remove a common operational dependency.

options.text: Shared expertise and resources may be valuable while the common provider creates concentrated exposure.
options.rationale: Benefits and common risk can coexist; neither cancels the need to examine the other.

options.text: Using multiple resellers establishes independent infrastructure in every case.
options.rationale: Commercial packaging does not establish distinct underlying routes or services.

options.text: Concentration means the service offers no useful capability.
options.rationale: A concentrated provider can supply valuable capability even while creating dependence.

section: Who owns the middle, again
objective: Represent an unverified upstream dependency honestly
stem: A retailer’s backup supplier declines to disclose its upstream route. The manager’s map shows it as completely independent because no shared carrier was named. How should the map change?

options.text: Mark the route as independent with a note that evidence is unnecessary.
options.rationale: Silence does not establish independence from the failure being considered.

options.text: Mark the route as certainly shared even though that is also unverified.
options.rationale: Lack of evidence does not establish either complete independence or a specific shared route.

options.text: Remove the supplier from the map so the uncertainty is less visible.
options.rationale: Omitting a real dependency hides a question that matters to the backup claim.

options.text: Mark the relevant dependency as unknown and seek confirmation or suitable evidence before relying on independence.
options.rationale: The map should distinguish established facts from an unanswered question.

section: Who owns the middle, again
objective: Distinguish an outage credit from restoration of a business outcome
stem: A booking provider offers a monthly fee credit after a qualifying outage. A salon manager treats this as a complete continuity plan. What is missing?

options.text: A plan for tolerable interruption and staff actions, because a credit does not complete missed bookings.
options.rationale: The financial remedy matters but does not itself preserve the business activity during the outage.

options.text: Proof that every credited outage must have caused no lost work.
options.rationale: A credit does not establish the extent of operational harm.

options.text: A requirement to remove all support commitments because credits are useless.
options.rationale: Contractual remedies can have value without replacing operational continuity planning.

options.text: An assumption that the booking service stays available whenever compensation is promised.
options.rationale: A promise about compensation is not a guarantee of uninterrupted operation.

section: Who owns the middle, again
objective: Scope dependency investigation around consequential work
stem: A small salon cannot investigate every supplier’s entire supply chain. Where should it start?

options.text: Map every possible global connection before considering any practical fallback.
options.rationale: Exhaustive mapping can consume effort without resolving the most important business risks.

options.text: Investigate the supplier with the most interesting equipment regardless of business reliance.
options.rationale: Technical interest does not identify which service failures stop important work.

options.text: Prioritise services whose loss stops important work and trace far enough to test the relevant backup claims.
options.rationale: This focuses limited effort on consequential dependencies while keeping unknowns visible.

options.text: Stop investigating beyond the contracted company because upstream suppliers are irrelevant.
options.rationale: A contracted service can depend on other organisations whose failure affects the business.

section: What a data centre is, for business purposes
objective: Identify an infrastructure dependency not established by equipment delivery
stem: A data-centre developer has servers arriving in September and promises to open then. The required local power upgrade is not yet scheduled. What should the manager establish before relying on that launch date?

options.text: Whether the server supplier can deliver more machines before September.
options.rationale: Additional machines do not establish that the power connection can support the launch.

options.text: When the necessary power service and other supporting infrastructure will actually be available.
options.rationale: Equipment delivery and usable supporting services have separate dependencies and timetables.

options.text: Whether the building has room for the full eventual server population.
options.rationale: Future floor space does not resolve the immediate power-readiness gap.

options.text: Whether the marketing team can announce September more prominently.
options.rationale: A stronger announcement does not supply evidence that the connection will be ready.

section: Read the unit before the headline
objective: Distinguish MW from MWh
stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a megawatt from a megawatt-hour?

options.text: MW measures energy over a month; MWh measures the number of customer connections.
options.rationale: Neither definition matches the units: MW is a rate and MWh is energy.

options.text: MW and MWh are alternative spellings for the same quantity.
options.rationale: A rate and the energy accumulated over time answer different questions.

options.text: MWh measures the peak rate, while MW measures total energy consumed.
options.rationale: This reverses the distinction.

options.text: MW measures a rate of supply or use; MWh measures energy over time.
options.rationale: One MW used steadily for one hour is one MWh.

section: Read the unit before the headline
objective: Calculate energy from stated actual use rather than connection capacity
stem: A cold-storage site has a connection capable of 8 MW but actually draws 3 MW steadily for 12 hours. How much energy does it use during those hours?

options.text: 36 MWh.
options.rationale: Actual power of 3 MW multiplied by 12 hours gives 36 MWh.

options.text: 96 MWh.
options.rationale: This multiplies the connection’s capacity by time instead of using the actual 3 MW draw.

options.text: 3 MWh.
options.rationale: This treats one hour’s energy at 3 MW as the total for all 12 hours.

options.text: 8 MWh.
options.rationale: Connection capacity is not itself a measure of energy consumed over the interval.

section: Read the unit before the headline
objective: Distinguish network-wide capacity from deliverable capacity at a site
stem: A utility reports spare capacity in another part of its network. A cold-storage operator assumes that its chosen site can therefore receive extra power immediately. What is missing?

options.text: Proof that every customer uses the same amount of power.
options.rationale: Equal customer use is not required to assess the route and upgrades serving this site.

options.text: A larger estimate of the operator’s future sales.
options.rationale: A sales forecast does not establish deliverable electrical capacity.

options.text: Evidence that the capacity can reach the site and what connection or network work is required.
options.rationale: Capacity has a location; usable supply depends on the infrastructure connecting it to the customer.

options.text: Confirmation that the spare capacity is described in GW rather than MW.
options.rationale: Changing the scale of the unit does not remove a delivery constraint.

section: Interest is not commitment
objective: Avoid treating alternative-site requests as additive committed load
stem: A developer asks about 20 MW at each of three sites but intends to build one facility. A planner records all three as 60 MW of committed future use. What should change?

options.text: Keep 60 MW because each submitted request is a separate promise to build.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly describes alternative sites rather than three committed facilities.

options.text: Link the requests to the one proposed project and record their stage before estimating committed load.
options.rationale: The relationship among requests matters; their sum is not automatically additive future demand.

options.text: Delete every request because alternative-site enquiries cannot be serious.
options.rationale: The interest may be real even though it is not a commitment to all sites.

options.text: Record 20 MW as electricity already consumed because one facility is intended.
options.rationale: An intended project is not actual consumption.

section: Interest is not commitment
objective: Distinguish energisation from a study or long-term full usage
stem: What does energisation establish in the chapter’s project sequence?

options.text: The connection has been made live.
options.rationale: Energisation is a connection milestone; it does not establish long-term use at full capacity.

options.text: The customer has used its full planned capacity for ten years.
options.rationale: Making a connection live does not establish future or past sustained full use.

options.text: A study has merely begun to investigate how the site could be served.
options.rationale: A load study and a live connection are different stages.

options.text: The customer has only expressed interest in one possible site.
options.rationale: An enquiry is earlier and less conclusive than energisation.

section: Interest is not commitment
objective: Investigate pipeline changes without assigning a cause from unlike totals
stem: An initial list totals 100 MW of cold-storage service requests; a later list totals 60 MW under signed agreements. A commentator says new terms caused 40 MW of viable demand to disappear. What evidence is needed?

options.text: Only the subtraction, because 100 minus 60 already establishes the cause.
options.rationale: The difference does not show which projects changed stage, consolidated, withdrew or obtained financing.

options.text: Only the later list’s larger number of signatures.
options.rationale: Signatures identify a stage but do not explain what happened to comparable earlier projects.

options.text: A comparison with unrelated requests from a different region and year.
options.rationale: A different population does not establish why these projects changed.

options.text: Follow comparable projects through the dates and stages, identifying withdrawals, timing changes, consolidation and financing outcomes.
options.rationale: Project-level evidence is needed to distinguish lost viable demand from other reasons the totals differ.

section: Who pays for the wire?
objective: Distinguish initial financing from ultimate cost responsibility
stem: A utility initially pays for an upgrade mainly intended for a cold-storage customer. An analyst concludes that utility shareholders must bear its entire final cost. What must be examined?

options.text: Only who signed the construction cheque.
options.rationale: Initial payment does not establish how the investment is recovered later.

options.text: Only the customer’s first month of actual electricity use.
options.rationale: One month of consumption does not reveal all payment obligations or approved cost allocation.

options.text: The applicable charges, agreements and regulatory allocation of the investment’s cost.
options.rationale: The party supplying money initially may differ from those expected to repay it through charges.

options.text: Whether the equipment has been installed, because installation fixes the ultimate payer.
options.rationale: Physical installation does not by itself settle the financing and recovery arrangements.

section: Who pays for the wire?
objective: Recognise a stranded asset that remains physically functional
stem: A purpose-built power upgrade works properly, but its intended customer cancels and no suitable replacement use is found. Revenue from the intended use cannot recover the investment. What makes this a potential stranded asset?

options.text: Its intended use no longer earns enough to recover the investment, even though the equipment works.
options.rationale: Stranding can be an economic problem rather than physical breakage.

options.text: It must contain a technical fault because no customer is using it.
options.rationale: A missing economic use does not establish an equipment fault.

options.text: It becomes costless once construction finishes.
options.rationale: The completed investment still has a cost and may still need funding or recovery.

options.text: It is necessarily fully recovered because it was built for a forecast customer.
options.rationale: A forecast does not guarantee the revenue or obligations needed to recover the cost.

section: Who pays for the wire?
objective: Explain how a minimum payment obligation changes forecast incentives
stem: A data-centre developer previously submitted requests without an associated payment obligation. A proposed agreement now requires a minimum payment even if actual use is lower. How does this change the planning relationship?

options.text: It converts the requested MW into a measured quantity of consumed energy.
options.rationale: A financial obligation is not actual electricity use.

options.text: It gives the developer a financial reason to test its forecast and gives the utility a firmer commitment than an enquiry.
options.rationale: The agreement connects a stated need with an obligation, improving the basis for planning without removing uncertainty.

options.text: It guarantees that the facility’s customers will pay enough to fund its obligations.
options.rationale: The agreement does not guarantee the developer’s business revenue.

options.text: It removes the need to assess infrastructure cost before construction.
options.rationale: Cost, timing and residual exposure still need examination.

section: Who pays for the wire?
objective: Identify residual exposure after a contract shifts some risk
stem: A utility says a data centre’s minimum-payment agreement has removed every risk of the proposed upgrade. Which assessment best corrects that claim?

options.text: All risk disappears once the agreement is signed, even before payments are collected.
options.rationale: A signed obligation can improve the planning basis without guaranteeing collection, construction cost or future use.

options.text: The minimum payment guarantees the customer cannot default, so only the equipment needs review.
options.rationale: An obligation to pay does not establish the customer’s continuing ability to pay.

options.text: Working equipment will recover its cost even if the customer leaves and no replacement use exists.
options.rationale: Physical function does not guarantee a revenue-producing use sufficient to recover the investment.

options.text: The customer could default, construction could overrun and the equipment could have limited alternative uses.
options.rationale: Contracts allocate responsibilities, but these uncertainties can leave exposure even with minimum charges.

section: What the Ohio terms actually teach
objective: Calculate demand and energy charges under a stated hypothetical contract
stem: Hypothetical contract, not AEP Ohio’s tariff: billable demand is the greater of an 8 MW floor and monthly measured peak. Demand costs $10 per kW per month; energy costs $50 per MWh. A facility draws 6 MW steadily for 30 days. Ignore other charges. What is the combined charge?

options.rationale: This is only the energy charge: 6 × 24 × 30 × $50. It omits the demand charge.
This adds a demand charge based on actual 6 MW, but the 8 MW floor applies.
Billable demand is 8,000 kW, costing $80,000. Energy is 4,320 MWh, costing $216,000; total $296,000.
This uses a 10 MW demand basis not established by the stated rule; the floor and measured peak determine the charge.

section: What the Ohio terms actually teach
objective: Apply a demand floor when measured peak exceeds it
stem: Hypothetical contract: billable demand is the greater of an 8 MW floor and monthly measured peak, at $10 per kW per month. A cold-storage site averages 4 MW but reaches a measured peak of 9 MW. What is its demand charge, excluding energy?

options.rationale: The 9 MW peak exceeds the floor, so 9,000 kW × $10 applies.
The floor is a minimum, not a ceiling; the higher measured peak controls here.
The stated demand rule uses peak demand, not the monthly average.
The rule chooses the greater of the floor and peak; it does not add them.

section: What the Ohio terms actually teach
objective: Assess cash exposure when revenue falls faster than usage-linked charges
stem: A cold-storage operator loses a major customer. Its energy use and energy charge fall, but its capacity-related minimum charge remains. The manager concludes that the lower bill means the contract can no longer cause cash-flow trouble. What is the flaw?

options.text: Lower energy use can never reduce any electricity charge.
options.rationale: Usage-linked energy charges can fall; the issue is what remains and how revenue changes.

options.text: A smaller bill may still be difficult to fund when revenue falls more and minimum obligations remain.
options.rationale: Affordability depends on cash inflows and the full continuing obligation, not merely a lower total bill.

options.text: The original customer request automatically cancels when energy use falls.
options.rationale: No cancellation right follows from lower use in the stated circumstances.

options.text: The remaining minimum charge proves the facility has consumed the reserved capacity.
options.rationale: A capacity-related payment obligation does not establish physical consumption.

section: Three positions, and the evidence each needs
objective: Choose evidence relevant to comparing customer treatment
stem: An industry group argues that two types of large electricity customer should not receive different service terms. What evidence most directly helps assess that position?

options.text: Whether the groups use equally fashionable technology.
options.rationale: Technology labels do not establish comparable infrastructure costs or financial risks.

options.text: Whether both groups prefer lower charges.
options.rationale: A shared preference does not show whether they impose comparable costs and exposure.

options.text: Whether the group’s statement uses stronger wording than the utility’s.
options.rationale: Persuasiveness does not establish the underlying cost comparison.

options.text: Whether the customers create comparable infrastructure costs, commitment patterns and risks.
options.rationale: Consistent treatment is assessed against relevant similarities and differences, not labels alone.

section: Three positions, and the evidence each needs
objective: Test a claim that stricter terms harm infrastructure cost recovery
stem: A policy advocate says stricter commitments drive away viable projects and leave remaining customers paying more. Which evidence would best test the full claim?

options.text: Which viable projects left because of the terms, where they could go, and which infrastructure costs remain or can be avoided.
options.rationale: The argument depends on behavioural responses and residual costs, not just a fall in requests.

options.text: Only the total number of early enquiries before the policy was announced.
options.rationale: Initial interest does not establish viable projects lost or the costs left behind.

options.text: Only the size of the largest proposed facility.
options.rationale: Project size alone does not establish the effect of the terms or the remaining exposure.

options.text: Only whether a developer publicly dislikes the policy.
options.rationale: Opposition is not evidence that a viable project departed or that net costs increased.

section: Three positions, and the evidence each needs
objective: Distinguish an appellant’s argument from an established finding
stem: In a fictional tariff dispute, an industry group’s appeal brief says the regulator lacked adequate evidence for separate terms. No court decision is supplied. How should a student describe this?

options.text: The court has found that the terms lacked evidence.
options.rationale: An appellant’s submission is not a court finding.

options.text: The regulator has admitted that its decision was unsupported.
options.rationale: The group’s allegation does not establish the regulator’s agreement.

options.text: The group argues that the evidence was inadequate; the assertion is not itself a judicial finding.
options.rationale: The claim must be attributed to the party making it, with the supplied record’s limits preserved.

options.text: The appeal proves the opposite position is correct because the group has an interest.
options.rationale: A party’s interest does not determine whether its argument is true or false.

section: Three positions, and the evidence each needs
objective: Evaluate screening and deterrence as effects requiring evidence
stem: A region considers stronger minimum commitments for new power connections. One official says they remove only speculative requests; another says they deter only valuable investment. What is the most defensible assessment?

options.text: The first claim must be right because a signed obligation guarantees a successful project.
options.rationale: An obligation does not guarantee commercial success, and strong terms may affect viable projects too.

options.text: Both screening and deterrence are possible; their scale and consequences need evidence about projects and costs.
options.rationale: The policy can change different kinds of project decisions, so a one-sided claim needs testing.

options.text: The second claim must be right because every enquiry represents a viable investment.
options.rationale: Enquiries can include alternatives and projects without secured financing.

options.text: The two claims can be settled by choosing whichever forecast is more optimistic.
options.rationale: Optimism does not establish the likelihood or cost of either effect.

section: Read a bill without inventing its cause
objective: Calculate a bill component without treating it as a causal explanation
stem: A fictional bill has $90 for supply, $35 for distribution, $20 for transmission-related charges and a $5 fixed charge. What share of its $150 total comes from the three non-supply lines?

options.rationale: That is the supply share: $90 divided by $150.
The three non-supply lines total $60, not $30.

options.text: About 66.7%.
options.rationale: This divides $60 by the $90 supply charge rather than by the full $150 bill.
The non-supply lines total $35 + $20 + $5 = $60; $60 divided by $150 is 40%.

section: Read a bill without inventing its cause
objective: Identify evidence needed to explain an increase in a bill line
stem: A fictional transmission-related charge rises by $5 while the other lines are unchanged. A neighbour attributes the increase to one new data centre. What can the bill alone establish?

options.text: The total rose by $5; attributing that change needs rate explanations and underlying cost evidence.
options.rationale: The amount can be calculated from the bill, but the cause requires information about the approved charge and costs.

options.text: The named data centre must have caused the increase because the line mentions transmission.
options.rationale: Transmission spending may have several purposes; the label does not identify that project as the cause.

options.text: The extra charge is necessarily unnecessary because it is not electricity supply.
options.rationale: Delivery infrastructure and services can create legitimate costs beyond supply.

options.text: The bill provides no usable information because it does not prove a cause.
options.rationale: It still establishes the line amounts and total change.

section: The question Chapter 4 left open
objective: Avoid extrapolating some unsuccessful AI pilots into all computing demand
stem: A manager cites several disappointing AI pilots as proof that all future data-centre demand will disappear. What does the reasoning omit?

options.text: Every AI pilot must succeed before a computing provider can have any customers.
options.rationale: Computing facilities serve many kinds of work; this universal requirement is unsupported.

options.text: A failed pilot necessarily means that its computing equipment stopped functioning.
options.rationale: A business result can disappoint even when the technology runs.

options.text: Data centres serve other work too, and the evidence about those pilots does not establish total future demand.
options.rationale: The claim extends beyond the population and work covered by its evidence.

options.text: Enthusiasm for AI guarantees that every proposed data centre will be fully occupied.
options.rationale: The opposite universal claim also lacks evidence about individual facilities and paying customers.

section: The question Chapter 4 left open
objective: Separate energy per task from aggregate energy use
stem: In a hypothetical comparison, a computing service performs twice as many identical tasks, using half as much electricity per task. All other electricity use is unchanged. What happens to electricity used for those tasks?

options.text: It halves because each task is more efficient.
options.rationale: This ignores the doubling in the number of tasks.

options.text: It stays the same because the volume increase offsets the lower electricity per task.
options.rationale: Twice the tasks multiplied by half the energy per task gives the original task-related total.

options.text: It doubles because the number of tasks doubles.
options.rationale: This ignores the reduction in electricity per task.

options.text: It proves that every data centre’s total demand will stay constant.
options.rationale: The calculation is conditional on the stated workload and does not establish a market-wide forecast.

section: The question Chapter 4 left open
objective: Preserve a project’s stage as information passes between organisations
stem: A developer’s spreadsheet lists “12 MW requested, financing not confirmed.” A computing provider copies the row into a report as “12 MW contracted and in use.” What should be corrected?

options.text: Only the unit should change to MWh, with the stage labels retained.
options.rationale: Changing a power unit does not fix the unsupported upgrade in commitment and usage status.

options.text: The original financing caveat should be deleted to make reports consistent.
options.rationale: Removing the qualification hides uncertainty instead of establishing the later stages.

options.text: The request should be counted as consumed power because the developer expects customers.
options.rationale: Expected customers do not establish a signed obligation or actual consumption.

options.text: Retain the request stage and financing qualification until evidence supports a commitment or actual use.
options.rationale: Information moving through the planning chain must not silently become more certain than its source.

section: Your turn
objective: Identify the tradeoff in a smaller first-phase capacity commitment
stem: A developer can commit to a smaller first phase and request more power later, but later capacity is not guaranteed. What tradeoff should it examine?

options.text: Lower initial commitment and exposure versus the risk of lacking capacity for a later business opportunity.
options.rationale: Phasing can preserve flexibility now while limiting assured expansion later.

options.text: A smaller first phase guarantees lower cost and unlimited future expansion.
options.rationale: The stated lack of guaranteed later capacity rules out that conclusion.

options.text: Reserving maximum capacity now removes every risk of future demand being lower.
options.rationale: A larger commitment does not make the business forecast certain.

options.text: The choice depends only on how many servers can be delivered this month.
options.rationale: Equipment delivery alone does not assess future demand, capacity availability or payment exposure.

section: A number that doubled every hundred days
objective: Identify unsupported extension of a short-period growth rate
stem: A network provider observes traffic doubling during a short launch period and extends that rate across every network for five years. What should a manager challenge first?

options.text: Whether doubling can ever be expressed mathematically.
options.rationale: The arithmetic can be valid even when the scope and persistence assumptions are unsupported.

options.text: Whether the measured population and period support the wider, longer forecast.
options.rationale: A short observation does not by itself establish sustained growth across other networks.

options.text: Whether higher traffic necessarily means the original observation was false.
options.rationale: Later growth would not establish that the earlier measurement was false.

options.text: Whether the provider should substitute revenue for traffic without changing its source data.
options.rationale: Relabelling traffic as revenue would mix distinct measures rather than validate the forecast.

section: What the money built
objective: Recognise competing investments aimed at the same expected market
stem: Three providers each plan enough capacity to serve most of the same forecast market. One manager treats the other announcements as independent proof that its own projected sales will occur. What is the flaw?

options.text: Competitors’ plans guarantee that the market will shrink.
options.rationale: Announcements do not establish either growth or contraction.

options.text: A real risk of being left behind removes the risk of building too much.
options.rationale: Both risks can exist at once.

options.text: Each provider’s capacity must serve a completely separate group of customers.
options.rationale: The scenario explicitly identifies the same expected market.

options.text: The plans may rely on overlapping demand and similar uncertain information.
options.rationale: Several investment decisions do not establish enough paying demand for each provider’s assumed share and price.

section: More use, less revenue
objective: Calculate revenue when volume grows and price falls
stem: A fictional computing service sells 1,000 units at $12 each, then 1,500 units at $6 each. What happens to revenue?

options.text: It falls from $12,000 to $9,000, a 25% decline.
options.rationale: Revenue is volume times price; the second period is $3,000 below the $12,000 starting value.

options.text: It rises by 50% because unit sales rise by 50%.
options.rationale: This ignores the lower price per unit.

options.text: It halves because price per unit halves.
options.rationale: This ignores the increase in unit sales.

options.text: It stays unchanged because more volume always offsets a price decline.
options.rationale: The stated multiplication gives different totals; offsetting is not automatic.

section: More use, less revenue
objective: Identify missing costs before turning revenue growth into a profit claim
stem: A computing service’s revenue rises by 20%. Its manager calls this proof of improved profit without reviewing the extra support and power needed. What remains to be established?

options.text: Whether unit sales can replace every cost measure.
options.rationale: Volume does not establish the resources consumed to serve it.

options.text: Whether a higher price was the only possible source of the revenue increase.
options.rationale: Revenue can rise through price or volume; neither alone settles profit.

options.text: How relevant costs changed alongside revenue.
options.rationale: Higher revenue can coexist with lower profit if costs rise sufficiently.

options.text: Whether the revenue should be renamed profit because customers paid it.
options.rationale: Receipts and revenue do not become profit without considering costs.

section: Follow the payment
objective: Distinguish financing from payment for services
stem: A computing operator receives $200,000 from a lender and $30,000 from customers for completed services. What distinction matters when assessing service demand?

options.text: Both receipts prove $230,000 of demand for the operator’s services.
options.rationale: The lender funded the business rather than purchasing the completed service.

options.text: The loan is financing; the customer receipts are evidence of payments for services.
options.rationale: The flows have different purposes and obligations even though both can increase cash.

options.text: The loan is operating profit because it arrived before expenses were paid.
options.rationale: Borrowed cash is not profit from supplying services.

options.text: Customer receipts are irrelevant whenever financing is available.
options.rationale: Customer payments remain central to whether the operation can justify and support its investment.

section: Follow the payment
objective: Limit what a supplier sale establishes about its buyer
stem: A design agency buys expensive workstations before securing clients. The equipment supplier reports the completed sale as revenue. What does that sale establish about the agency’s future return?

options.text: The agency has already earned revenue equal to the purchase price.
options.rationale: Buying equipment is not the agency’s sale of design services.

options.text: The agency will recover its investment because the supplier made a sale.
options.rationale: The supplier’s transaction does not establish future paying clients or the agency’s costs.

options.text: The purchase is necessarily suspicious because the agency has not yet secured clients.
options.rationale: Businesses can legitimately invest before demand is fully established; the return remains uncertain.

options.text: The supplier completed a sale, while the agency still needs a viable service business to earn a return.
options.rationale: One company’s revenue can precede evidence of successful customer economics for another.

section: Follow the payment
objective: Distinguish a valuation change from an actual financing transaction
stem: The publicly traded supplier of a design agency’s equipment rises in stock-market value. The agency’s manager says this gives the agency more cash for expansion. What is missing?

options.text: An actual financing or payment transaction that supplies cash to the agency.
options.rationale: A supplier’s share-price increase does not automatically transfer cash into its customer’s account.

options.text: A calculation multiplying the agency’s equipment cost by the supplier’s share-price gain.
options.rationale: That calculation does not create a cash transfer.

options.text: A decision to record the supplier’s market gain as the agency’s service revenue.
options.rationale: The agency did not earn that gain by supplying services.

options.text: Proof that the supplier’s shareholders all use the agency’s services.
options.rationale: Shareholder identity does not establish an expansion-financing transaction.

section: One purchase, two sets of accounts
objective: Calculate the cash gap after an equipment purchase
stem: A fictional operator pays $120,000 cash for equipment at the start of a year, collects $60,000 from services and pays $36,000 in cash operating costs. There are no other cash flows. What is the net cash change including equipment?

options.text: A $24,000 increase.
options.rationale: This is receipts minus operating payments before the equipment purchase, which the question includes.

options.text: Zero, because the equipment remains an asset.
options.rationale: Owning an asset does not reverse the cash paid to acquire it.

options.text: A $96,000 decrease.
options.rationale: $60,000 − $36,000 − $120,000 = −$96,000; existing cash or financing is needed to cover the gap.

options.text: A $120,000 decrease.
options.rationale: This includes the purchase but omits the $24,000 net cash generated by services before that purchase.

section: One purchase, two sets of accounts
objective: Calculate profit with depreciation rather than immediate expensing of the full purchase
stem: A fictional operator buys $120,000 of equipment, puts it in service immediately and initially estimates a six-year useful life with no residual value. Straight-line depreciation applies. Annual service revenue is $60,000 and operating expense is $36,000. Ignore taxes, financing and other items. What is annual accounting profit?

options.rationale: This deducts the whole equipment purchase immediately instead of the stated annual depreciation.

options.text: $4,000 profit.
$24,000 profit.
options.rationale: This omits depreciation.

options.text: $20,000 profit.
options.rationale: This is the annual depreciation amount, not revenue less the stated expenses.

section: One purchase, two sets of accounts
objective: Distinguish the purposes of the three financial statements
stem: Which mapping correctly identifies the main questions answered by the statements described in the chapter?

options.text: Income statement: bank movements; cash-flow statement: asset lives; balance sheet: sales during the year.
options.rationale: This confuses period performance, cash movements and the position at a date.

options.text: Income statement: company market price; cash-flow statement: customer forecasts; balance sheet: only equipment.
options.rationale: These are not the stated purposes of the three statements.

options.text: All three report the same profit figure with different layouts.
options.rationale: They answer different questions rather than presenting interchangeable measures.

options.text: Income statement: revenue and expenses over a period; cash-flow statement: cash movements; balance sheet: assets, obligations and equity at a date.
options.rationale: The statements distinguish performance, cash movement and financial position.

section: One purchase, two sets of accounts
objective: Explain how delayed collection affects cash without changing earned revenue under stated assumptions
stem: A design agency earns $50,000 of service revenue but collects $40,000 by year-end. The remaining $10,000 is collectible, and expenses and all other conditions are unchanged. Compared with collecting the full amount, what changes?

options.text: Cash receipts are $10,000 lower, while the unpaid $10,000 is a receivable and earned revenue is unchanged.
options.rationale: An amount owed by customers is an asset, not cash available today; the stated revenue was still earned.

options.text: Earned revenue automatically falls to $40,000 solely because collection is delayed.
options.rationale: The question states that $50,000 was earned and the unpaid balance is collectible.

options.text: The bank balance is unchanged because a receivable can be counted as cash.
options.rationale: A receivable is not yet a cash receipt.

options.text: The unpaid $10,000 must be added to profit a second time.
options.rationale: The amount is already included in earned revenue; counting it again would duplicate it.

section: An assumption changes profit
objective: Interpret the effect of alternative initial useful-life assumptions
stem: Compare two initial estimates for the same $120,000 equipment purchase: six years or ten years, straight-line depreciation with no residual value. Receipts and cash operating costs are identical, with no tax or financing effects. What changes under the ten-year estimate?

options.text: Annual cash receipts rise by $8,000 because depreciation is lower.
options.rationale: A depreciation assumption does not produce new customer receipts.

options.text: The original cash purchase falls from $120,000 to $72,000.
options.rationale: The equipment payment is the same under both assumptions.

options.text: Annual depreciation falls from $20,000 to $12,000 and profit rises by $8,000, while the stated cash flows are unchanged.
options.rationale: The estimate changes the annual expense allocation, not these receipts or payments.

options.text: The longer estimate proves the equipment will remain commercially useful for ten years.
options.rationale: An accounting estimate needs operational support; it does not guarantee future usefulness.

section: An assumption changes profit
objective: Assess an estimate using evidence rather than presuming honesty or fraud
stem: A warehouse plans to use a longer initial life for new sorting equipment because similar equipment has remained useful longer. What should a reviewer examine?

options.text: Only whether a longer life increases reported profit, since that proves fraud.
options.rationale: A favourable effect is not itself proof of wrongdoing.

options.text: Operating evidence for the expected useful life and clear disclosure of the estimate’s effect.
options.rationale: A defensible estimate needs support; its effect on profit should be understood rather than automatically accepted or condemned.

options.text: Only whether management calls it an accounting choice, since that makes it acceptable.
options.rationale: A label does not make unsupported treatment defensible.

options.text: Whether the longer life can eliminate the original cash payment from the cash-flow statement.
options.rationale: The estimate does not undo the purchase payment.

section: Buying equipment is not renting a service
objective: Calculate the simplified result of buying a service instead of equipment
stem: A design agency collects and earns $60,000 during the year, pays and expenses $35,000 of other operating costs, and pays $28,000 for a year’s computing service expensed as consumed. It buys no equipment. Ignore tax, financing and other transactions. What are its profit and net cash change?

options.text: $25,000 profit and a $25,000 cash increase.
options.rationale: This omits the computing service payment and expense.

options.text: A $3,000 loss but a $25,000 cash increase.
options.rationale: The $28,000 service payment affects cash as well as expense under the stated timing.

options.text: Zero profit because rented computing must be recorded as owned equipment.
options.rationale: The stated arrangement is a service expensed as consumed, not a purchase of equipment.

options.text: A $3,000 loss and a $3,000 cash decrease.
options.rationale: Both equal $60,000 − $35,000 − $28,000 under the stated matched earning and payment timing.

section: Cash is patient. Debt has dates.
objective: Compare cash available with a dated principal repayment
stem: An operator generates $24,000 cash before capital spending and must repay $30,000 of loan principal this year. There is no other available cash or financing. Before interest or new purchases, what does this imply?

options.text: A $6,000 cash gap; principal repayment is a cash use rather than an operating expense.
options.rationale: The available $24,000 is short of the $30,000 commitment even before additional cash needs.

options.text: No gap because principal is not an operating expense.
options.rationale: Not being an operating expense does not remove the required cash payment.

options.text: A $6,000 accounting loss follows automatically from subtracting principal from operating profit.
options.rationale: The stated comparison concerns cash, and principal repayment is not treated as operating expense.

options.text: The repayment can be counted as new funding for the operator.
options.rationale: Repaying principal sends cash out rather than supplying it.

section: Cash is patient. Debt has dates.
objective: Separate financing runway from the investment’s economic merit
stem: A profitable distribution business can fund a new warehouse-automation service for several years, although that service has not shown an acceptable return. What does the available funding establish?

options.text: The new service must be economically worthwhile because another business can pay for it.
options.rationale: Ability to fund an activity does not establish its return.

options.text: The new service must fail because it initially uses funds from another operation.
options.rationale: Cross-funding can support a useful investment; it does not determine the eventual outcome.

options.text: The firm may be able to wait longer, but the new service’s return and the opportunity cost still need examination.
options.rationale: Survival while learning and economic justification are separate questions.

options.text: The original business’s cash has no alternative use, so its allocation requires no decision.
options.rationale: Cash can have other uses, and the source business may also weaken.

section: Cash is patient. Debt has dates.
objective: Identify a supplier’s exposure when it finances the buyer
stem: An equipment supplier helps finance a warehouse operator’s purchase. Which additional question should a manager ask when interpreting the supplier’s sales growth?

options.text: Whether financing makes repayment independent of the warehouse’s performance.
options.rationale: The buyer’s ability to pay can remain central to the supplier’s exposure.

options.text: Whether the operator’s customer receipts can support repayment or further financing is needed.
options.rationale: A financed sale can leave the supplier exposed to the buyer’s future cash generation.

options.text: Whether a financed sale is automatically fraudulent.
options.rationale: Vendor financing can support legitimate transactions; its risks need assessment.

options.text: Whether customer use alone can be substituted for repayment in cash.
options.rationale: Usage does not meet a cash obligation unless it results in sufficient receipts.

section: Cash is patient. Debt has dates.
objective: Evaluate staged capacity against paid demand and expansion lead time
stem: An operator proposes adding equipment in phases rather than making one large purchase. Which evidence best informs that choice?

options.text: Only the number of enquiries, treating each as a paid order.
options.rationale: Interest does not establish committed demand or cash receipts.

options.text: Only the equipment supplier’s advertised market growth.
options.rationale: A supplier’s forecast does not settle this operator’s customers, cash timing or expansion constraints.

options.text: Only whether buying everything now produces a larger accounting asset.
options.rationale: Asset size does not establish that the commitment fits demand or financing.

options.text: Paying customer commitments, cash timing and how quickly the next capacity increment can be added.
options.rationale: Phasing preserves cash but can sacrifice the ability to meet a sudden increase in demand.

section: What can wait for demand?
objective: Distinguish economic obsolescence from physical failure
stem: Which situation best illustrates economic obsolescence?

options.text: Equipment still functions but is costly to operate relative to newer alternatives.
options.rationale: The economic attractiveness can decline without a physical failure.

options.text: Equipment stops functioning because an essential component breaks.
options.rationale: This describes physical failure.

options.text: An invoice remains unpaid for a service already delivered.
options.rationale: This concerns collection and a receivable rather than equipment obsolescence.

options.text: A company receives new cash from investors.
options.rationale: This is a financing event, not a loss of an asset’s economic usefulness.

section: What can wait for demand?
objective: Assess reuse and adaptation rather than assuming long physical life guarantees recovery
stem: A purpose-built automated warehouse may stand for decades, but its intended customer cancels. Another customer would require expensive alterations. What should the owner examine?

options.text: Only the building’s remaining physical life.
options.rationale: Longevity does not establish paying demand or affordable adaptation.

options.text: Only the original construction price as proof of its current earning ability.
options.rationale: Historical expenditure does not show what the asset can earn now.

options.text: Alternative uses, adaptation costs, likely paying demand and commitments that remain while it waits.
options.rationale: Recoverability depends on useful economic applications and costs, not just physical survival.

options.text: Whether cancelling the original customer erases the owner’s existing commitments.
options.rationale: The customer’s departure does not by itself remove the owner’s obligations.

section: Your instrument panel
objective: Reconcile scope and periods before comparing supplier and buyer growth rates
stem: A supplier’s reported data-centre revenue grows faster than several operators’ announced total capital budgets. An analyst declares the reports inconsistent. What needs checking first?

options.text: Whether all the percentages can be averaged into one industry-growth number.
options.rationale: Averaging does not reconcile different populations, periods or transaction types.

options.text: Reporting periods, products, customer groups, intermediaries and delivery or spending timing.
options.rationale: The reports may not describe the same transactions, so differing growth rates do not establish a contradiction.

options.text: Whether the supplier’s larger percentage should replace every operator’s report.
options.rationale: A larger figure is not more authoritative when scope differs.

options.text: Whether announced budgets can always be treated as completed supplier sales.
options.rationale: Plans and completed transactions can differ in scope and timing.

section: Your instrument panel
objective: Investigate a gap between revenue growth and customer cash collection
stem: A design agency reports growing service revenue, but cash receipts lag and receivables rise. Which records should a manager connect to understand the pressure on cash?

options.text: Only share-price charts for the agency’s software suppliers.
options.rationale: Those charts do not explain whether the agency’s customers paid.

options.text: Only equipment serial numbers and depreciation schedules.
options.rationale: These concern assets, not collection of the growing service revenue.

options.text: Only forecasts of next year’s customer count.
options.rationale: Forecasts do not establish the status of current unpaid invoices.

options.text: Service and billing records with collection dates, amounts due and customer payment terms.
options.rationale: Linking sales to receipts distinguishes delayed collection from other explanations for cash pressure.

section: Your instrument panel
objective: Test whether an accounting life has a business explanation
stem: An operator’s investment case assumes processors earn revenue for ten years, but operations can identify paying uses only for the first four. What should the reviewer ask for?

options.text: Evidence of plausible later-year work, its economics and any replacement or adaptation spending.
options.rationale: The expected earning life should support the accounting and investment assumptions rather than merely repeat them.

options.text: A ten-year depreciation label as sufficient proof of later customer demand.
options.rationale: An expense-allocation assumption does not establish earning capacity.

options.text: An immediate fraud finding solely because the operating forecast is shorter.
options.rationale: The mismatch warrants investigation; it is not itself proof of fraud.

options.text: A forecast of industry traffic with no link to the equipment’s later uses.
options.rationale: Aggregate adoption does not show that these assets will earn enough for this operator.

section: Your turn
objective: Handle an undisclosed figure without inventing precision
stem: A student reviewing a design company’s annual report cannot find equipment purchases separately disclosed from a broader investment line. What is the appropriate treatment?

options.text: Assume the entire broader line is equipment and present it without qualification.
options.rationale: That substitutes an unverified component estimate for a disclosed figure.

options.text: Use the equipment supplier’s revenue as the company’s purchase total.
options.rationale: The supplier’s revenue covers a different set of transactions and customers.

options.text: Record the exact disclosed label and period, and state that equipment purchases are not separately identified.
options.rationale: This preserves what the source supports and makes the limitation visible.

options.text: Estimate a convenient number and label it “reported.”
options.rationale: An estimate must not be represented as a disclosed fact.

section: A contractor's account in Pennsylvania
objective: Verify a sensitive request through an independent contact route
stem: A retailer receives a familiar-looking supplier email asking for new payment details. What should the employee do before making the change?

options.text: Reply to the email asking the sender to confirm the request.
options.rationale: A reply could reach the same person who sent a deceptive message.

options.text: Check through an independently known supplier contact and report the suspicious request through the normal channel.
options.rationale: Independent verification avoids relying on contact details supplied by the potentially deceptive message.

options.text: Use the telephone number in the email because a call is safer than a reply.
options.rationale: The sender may control that number too; the contact route must be independently known.

options.text: Approve the change if the message includes the correct supplier logo.
options.rationale: A familiar logo does not establish who sent the request.

section: A contractor's account in Pennsylvania
objective: Avoid adding potentially overlapping exposure populations
stem: A fictional retailer reports exposure of 12,000 payment-card accounts and personal details for 18,000 customers. It has not established the overlap or how many accounts each customer holds. What can a manager report?

options.text: Exactly 30,000 people were affected.
options.rationale: The measures concern accounts and customers, and their overlap is unknown.

options.text: Exactly 18,000 people were affected because the larger figure includes the smaller one.
options.rationale: The report does not establish that inclusion.

options.text: Exactly 6,000 additional people were affected beyond the card-account group.
options.rationale: Subtracting different, unreconciled populations does not identify additional people.

options.text: The two reported exposure measures separately, with the unique-person total still unresolved.
options.rationale: Keeping the measures distinct preserves what the evidence establishes without inventing a population count.

section: The detail that should bother you most
objective: Supply the context and escalation route an alert requires
stem: A clinic analyst sees an overnight supplier login alert but cannot find a work schedule or anyone authorised to interrupt access. Which improvement most directly addresses this response gap?

options.text: Make scheduled work, access scope and an authorised escalation contact available to the analyst.
options.rationale: The analyst needs business context and a route to a decision, not just the alert.

options.text: Increase the number of alerts sent to the same unattended queue.
options.rationale: More notifications do not supply the missing context or authority.

options.text: Treat every overnight supplier login as confirmed misuse.
options.rationale: An unusual time warrants assessment but does not prove an attack.

options.text: Ask the analyst to wait until the supplier reports a problem.
options.rationale: That substitutes supplier reporting for the clinic’s own timely assessment.

section: What access are you approving?
objective: Limit permissions to the supplier’s business task
stem: A refrigeration contractor needs to read equipment status and submit repair reports. Which access approval best fits that work?

options.text: All warehouse applications, because the contractor works at the warehouse.
options.rationale: Physical location does not justify access to unrelated business functions.

options.text: Customer payment records as well, provided the password is strong.
options.rationale: Password strength does not make unnecessary permissions appropriate.

options.text: Equipment status and repair reporting, excluding unrelated payment and dispatch functions.
options.rationale: Least privilege limits what the account can do to what its work requires.

options.text: The previous contractor’s permissions without checking the new agreement.
options.rationale: Inherited permissions may exceed or fail to match the new work.

section: What access are you approving?
objective: Separate identity checks from permission limits
stem: A clinic adds multifactor authentication to a maintenance supplier’s account, which still has unnecessary access to patient billing records. What remains to be done?

options.text: Share the account among technicians so everyone uses the stronger sign-in.
options.rationale: Sharing reduces individual accountability and leaves excessive permissions unchanged.

options.text: Remove unnecessary permissions; the extra sign-in check does not correct them.
options.rationale: Authentication helps establish identity, while permissions govern what an authenticated account can do.

options.text: Keep the permissions because a second authentication factor makes them harmless.
options.rationale: Stronger authentication does not justify broader access after login.

options.text: Replace access review with a longer password-expiry schedule.
options.rationale: Password timing does not establish which records the supplier needs.

section: What access are you approving?
objective: Identify what makes segmentation an effective boundary
stem: What makes segmentation useful for limiting movement between systems?

options.text: Giving each application a different name.
options.rationale: Different names do not limit connections or permissions.

options.text: Drawing separate boxes on the organisation’s systems diagram.
options.rationale: A diagram describes intended separation but does not enforce it.

options.text: Assigning all systems to the same business owner.
options.rationale: Ownership helps accountability but does not itself restrict communication.

options.text: Controlling the actual connections and permissions across system boundaries.
options.rationale: Segmentation depends on what systems can reach and communicate with, not their labels.

section: What access are you approving?
objective: Make temporary access accountable and time-limited
stem: A distributor approves extra access for a contractor’s weekend repair. What should accompany the approval?

options.text: The added scope, approver, expiry and person responsible for confirming removal.
options.rationale: These make the exception explicit and prevent temporary access from becoming indefinite.

options.text: A note saying “temporary” with removal left to the contractor’s discretion.
options.rationale: The label alone supplies neither a deadline nor accountable confirmation.

options.text: A permanent administrator role so future urgent repairs need no review.
options.rationale: This expands the exception beyond the stated work and period.

options.text: An agreement to revisit access only if an alert occurs.
options.rationale: Unneeded access remains a risk even when no alert has occurred.

section: What a breach costs the business
objective: Distinguish confidentiality, integrity and availability
stem: Which description correctly distinguishes the three kinds of information-system harm?

options.text: Confidentiality concerns uptime; integrity concerns access speed; availability concerns accuracy.
options.rationale: This confuses usable service with protection against disclosure and alteration.

options.text: All three concern whether someone can sign in successfully.
options.rationale: Successful sign-in does not establish that records are private or unaltered.

options.text: Confidentiality concerns who can see information; integrity concerns unauthorised change; availability concerns use when needed.
options.rationale: These distinguish disclosure, trust in records and access to service.

options.text: Confidentiality concerns passwords only; integrity concerns hardware only; availability concerns backups only.
options.rationale: Each concept applies more broadly than a particular control or component.

section: What a breach costs the business
objective: Recognise an integrity problem despite continued availability
stem: A distributor’s order system remains online, but delivery addresses have been changed without authorisation. Which immediate business concern does this illustrate?

options.text: Availability alone, because the system has users.
options.rationale: The system is available; the reported problem is unauthorised alteration of records.

options.text: Integrity: staff may act on altered records even though the service works.
options.rationale: Online access does not make the order data trustworthy.

options.text: Confidentiality alone, because every record change proves data was copied.
options.rationale: Unauthorised change does not by itself establish disclosure.

options.text: No information-system harm unless dispatch stops.
options.rationale: Wrong addresses can cause harm while the application remains operational.

section: What a breach costs the business
objective: Reconcile cost scope before combining reported amounts
stem: A retailer’s incident summary lists a recovery estimate, paid repair invoices and an insurance reimbursement. The estimate may already include those invoices. How should a manager assess the financial impact?

options.text: Add all three as costs because each relates to the incident.
options.rationale: That may double-count recovery work and treat a reimbursement as another cost.

options.text: Use only the reimbursement because it represents the final cost.
options.rationale: A reimbursement need not cover all losses or define their scope.

options.text: Treat the estimate and invoices as separate losses because their labels differ.
options.rationale: Different labels do not prove that the underlying work is different.

options.text: Check covered work and periods, identify overlap, and distinguish gross costs from reimbursement.
options.rationale: A defensible total requires consistent scope and treatment of incoming and outgoing amounts.

section: What a breach costs the business
objective: Include operational and customer burdens beyond incident invoices
stem: A retailer measures incident harm only by its technical repair bill. Customer-service staff have postponed other work, and affected customers must replace cards. What is missing from the assessment?

options.text: Diverted staff effort and customer burdens, even where no repair invoice records them.
options.rationale: Business consequences include internal opportunity costs and effects on others.

options.text: Nothing, because only payments to technical suppliers count as harm.
options.rationale: Important consequences need not appear in a supplier invoice.

options.text: A fixed reputation charge equal to the repair bill.
options.rationale: The chapter offers no basis for inventing a numerical reputation cost.

options.text: Proof that every delayed project permanently lost its entire value.
options.rationale: That overstates the evidence rather than recognising the actual disruption.

section: Now the version with no attacker
objective: Identify a shared dependency that defeats a fallback
stem: A clinic’s main reception computers and designated spare computers receive the same update at the same time. Both become unusable. What should the recovery-planning review address?

options.text: Whether labelling the spares as emergency equipment would have protected them.
options.rationale: A label does not remove a shared failure dependency.
