options.text: An agreed authoritative record and a process to reconcile changed transactions during fallback.
options.rationale: Returning to old software does not resolve divergent order states.

options.text: A promise that the older system will automatically know every new-system change.
options.rationale: That behaviour must be established, not assumed.

options.text: A decision to discard every order entered after launch.
options.rationale: Discarding valid transactions can create lost orders and customer harm.

options.text: Only a shorter message announcing the switch.
options.rationale: Communication does not reconcile records or assign recovery work.

section: Listen to the person who objects
objective: Turn an employee objection into an examined workflow requirement
stem: An experienced employee says the proposed workflow locks delivery addresses before legitimate last-minute changes occur. What should the manager do?

options.text: Reject the objection as resistance because the employee knows the old system.
options.rationale: Experience can reveal a real step the design missed.

options.text: Give everyone unrestricted ability to change all records.
options.rationale: A legitimate amendment need does not justify removing unrelated controls.

options.text: Examine representative cases and test a controlled amendment process against the business need.
options.rationale: The objection supplies evidence to investigate without giving it an automatic veto.

options.text: Preserve every old step in custom code before asking why it exists.
options.rationale: Some old steps may be unnecessary; each needs a business purpose.

section: Listen to the person who objects
objective: Make the cost and release impact of added scope explicit
stem: A hotel project is ready to pilot booking and billing when managers request a loyalty platform too. What question best controls the change?

options.text: Can it be called a small enhancement so the schedule stays unchanged on paper?
options.rationale: Renaming added work does not remove its costs or dependencies.

options.text: What problem does it solve, is it needed for the first release, and which cost, training or schedule commitments must change?
options.rationale: A reasonable addition still needs an explicit scope decision and resource tradeoff.

options.text: Should every new request be accepted because users asked for it?
options.rationale: Individually useful requests can collectively exceed the project’s capacity.

options.text: Should all future improvements be permanently forbidden?
options.rationale: Scope control allows considered changes rather than imposing an absolute ban.

section: Listen to the person who objects
objective: Distinguish configuration from customisation and recognise maintenance implications
stem: Which distinction matches the chapter?

options.text: Configuration always requires new code; customisation uses only existing settings.
options.rationale: This reverses the distinction.

options.text: Configuration and customisation both guarantee compatibility with every upgrade.
options.rationale: Compatibility needs evaluation, especially for extensions.

options.text: Customisation is always wrong because every old process must be abandoned.
options.rationale: Custom work can be justified by a genuine need.

options.text: Configuration uses supported options; customisation extends behaviour and may require additional maintenance and upgrade testing.
options.rationale: The distinction helps identify ongoing ownership and compatibility work.

section: The cost of leaving starts before arrival
objective: Convert an exit allowance into an operationally usable exit plan
stem: A distributor budgets $10,000 for exit but has no agreement about transaction history, linked attachments, continued access or transition assistance. What remains unresolved?

options.text: Whether it can obtain and use the records it needs, on what terms, and with what transition work.
options.rationale: A monetary allowance does not establish the practical ability or contractual arrangements to leave.

options.text: Nothing, because budgeting an exit amount creates a right to all needed services.
options.rationale: An allowance is not a supplier commitment or legal entitlement.

options.text: Only whether a customer-name list can be downloaded.
options.rationale: Names alone may not reconstruct relationships, orders or history.

options.text: Whether dependence proves the purchase can never be worthwhile.
options.rationale: A useful purchase can create acceptable dependence if that dependence is understood and managed.

section: Ask the adviser for a recommendation—and its limits
objective: Make an adviser’s recommendation conditional on unresolved evidence
stem: A consultant recommends a distributor’s new service but has not tested billing integration. How should the manager use the recommendation?

options.text: Treat the consultant’s confidence as proof that integration will work within budget.
options.rationale: Confidence does not replace the missing test.

options.text: Reject all advice because consultants may have incentives.
options.rationale: Incentives and scope deserve examination but do not make advice useless.

options.text: Record the integration assumption, identify evidence that would change the recommendation and assign an owner to resolve it.
options.rationale: Useful advice makes dependencies and uncertainty visible without removing managerial ownership.

options.text: Remove integration from the estimate so the recommendation has no stated uncertainty.
options.rationale: Concealing an assumption does not eliminate its risk or cost.

section: The question you have been carrying
objective: Preserve an earlier claim when updating a decision record
stem: A campus-club officer predicted that a booking tool would remove all scheduling errors. New evidence shows fewer errors but continuing exceptions. How should the officer update the record?

options.text: Replace the original prediction with “fewer errors” so the record matches the evidence.
options.rationale: That erases the difference between the earlier claim and later learning.

options.text: Keep the original claim and add the evidence, revised interpretation, next action and review date.
options.rationale: An intact history makes the change in reasoning visible.

options.text: Keep only the original claim because revising a prediction shows inconsistency.
options.rationale: Responding to evidence can improve a judgment without concealing the original.

options.text: Report complete success because the tool reduced at least some errors.
options.rationale: A partial improvement does not establish the original absolute claim.

section: The question you have been carrying
objective: Record an evidence gap rather than manufacture an update
stem: A distributor analyst reaches a scheduled review of a technology forecast but has no new evidence. What is the appropriate entry?

options.text: Write that the forecast was confirmed because nothing disproved it.
options.rationale: Lack of new evidence does not establish confirmation.

options.text: Invent a plausible performance estimate to keep the record useful.
options.rationale: An invented estimate would misrepresent what has been learned.

options.text: Delete the review date until a favourable result appears.
options.rationale: This undermines the planned review and hides uncertainty.

options.text: State that no new evidence is available, identify what remains unresolved and set the next review.
options.rationale: The record can honestly preserve uncertainty and a plan to revisit it.

section: The handoff, one more time
objective: Replace lost beginner learning opportunities with supported practice
stem: A distributor uses a tool to produce first drafts that junior staff previously prepared. What should a manager ask about their development?

options.text: Where juniors will now receive supervised practice, experienced guidance and feedback on decisions.
options.rationale: Faster production does not automatically replace the learning previously embedded in the task.

options.text: Whether faster draft production proves juniors now understand the business better.
options.rationale: Output speed does not establish understanding.

options.text: Whether all entry-level roles must disappear once drafts are automated.
options.rationale: The chapter does not support a universal employment prediction.

options.text: Whether feedback can be removed because the tool supplies polished wording.
options.rationale: Polish does not replace practice in judging evidence and consequences.

section: What to practise when the future is uncertain
objective: Make an uncertain recommendation actionable and reviewable
stem: A distributor analyst recommends trying a revised order-checking process, while acknowledging uncertain staff effort. What makes the recommendation actionable?

options.text: A confident statement that the new process must work.
options.rationale: Confidence does not allocate work or resolve the uncertainty.

options.text: A list of every imaginable risk with no proposed action.
options.rationale: The list leaves the decision and follow-through unspecified.

options.text: A bounded action, responsible owner, expected consequence and evidence or date for reconsideration.
options.rationale: These connect the judgment to implementation and review.

options.text: An instruction to let the software decide who is responsible.
options.rationale: Software does not remove the need for organisational ownership.

section: What to practise when the future is uncertain
objective: Seek decision-changing evidence rather than use analysis to defer a choice
stem: A campus club has enough evidence to choose a small, reversible booking trial. An officer asks for a year-long industry survey but cannot explain how it would change the choice. What is the most useful response?

options.text: Delay until every uncertainty about the industry is resolved.
options.rationale: That standard may prevent any timely decision without improving this choice.

options.text: Identify the remaining evidence that could change the decision and use a bounded trial if it can resolve the relevant uncertainty.
options.rationale: Further analysis should serve the decision rather than become a reason to avoid it.

options.text: Ignore all uncertainty because the trial is small.
options.rationale: A reversible step still needs limits, a purpose and review.

options.text: Treat any request for more evidence as resistance and reject it.
options.rationale: Some missing evidence matters; the issue is its relevance to the choice.

section: What to practise when the future is uncertain
objective: Compare conflicting evidence instead of letting one favourable result settle approval
stem: A distributor’s proposed tool performs well technically and is affordable, but its workflow leaves nobody responsible for disputed orders. What should the analyst recommend?

options.text: Approve because technical performance is the strongest evidence available.
options.rationale: Technical success does not resolve the operational ownership gap.

options.text: Approve because an affordable service cannot create a business problem.
options.rationale: Low cost does not make the workflow workable.

options.text: Reject all technology purchases until uncertainty is eliminated.
options.rationale: The specific gap may be resolvable without demanding certainty about everything.

options.text: Resolve and test the responsibility for disputes before treating the arrangement as ready.
options.rationale: The decision must connect technical and financial evidence to the people and process needed for the work.

section: What to practise when the future is uncertain
objective: Follow a recommendation through to an owned outcome check
stem: A campus club approves a new booking process, but nobody is assigned to implement it or check whether missed bookings decline. What is missing from the recommendation?

options.text: A stronger claim that the tool will transform the club.
options.rationale: Stronger wording does not supply responsibility or outcome evidence.

options.text: A longer list of product features.
options.rationale: Features do not assign implementation or establish improvement.

options.text: Named responsibility for action and a defined check of whether the intended outcome occurs.
options.rationale: Accountability includes carrying the recommendation into its consequences and reviewing the result.

options.text: A promise that the original recommendation can never be reconsidered.
options.rationale: New evidence may require a change, so review should remain possible.

section: Get close to a decision
objective: Identify the three connected parts of the chapter’s learning plan
stem: Which sequence describes the chapter’s practical learning plan?

options.text: Observe a decision, verify a claim and defend a piece of work.
options.rationale: The sequence connects understanding a choice to checking evidence and receiving challenge.

options.text: Predict an industry winner, memorise its slogans and repeat its forecast.
options.rationale: This does not build independent verification or defensible work.

options.text: Collect software names, rank their popularity and select the newest.
options.rationale: Product familiarity alone does not establish decision quality.

options.text: Read a summary, accept its claims and avoid disagreement.
options.rationale: That omits verification and the feedback needed to improve reasoning.

section: Get close to a decision
objective: Define a learning task small and specific enough to complete
stem: A student wants to learn from a campus club’s booking decision. Which plan best turns that aspiration into practical work?

options.text: Become an expert on all event technology before the semester ends.
options.rationale: The scope is too broad and does not identify a concrete piece of work or feedback.

options.text: Read whenever time permits and wait for confidence to develop.
options.rationale: There is no defined task, completion date or review of the work.

options.text: By Friday, use an approved account of the choice to check one price claim, write a short comparison and ask the treasurer for feedback.
options.rationale: The plan names observable work, evidence, a deadline and a person who can challenge it.

options.text: Join every private meeting so the account contains as much detail as possible.
options.rationale: Learning does not justify unapproved access to confidential discussions.

section: Get close to a decision
objective: Separate a decision-maker’s explanation from an observer’s inference
stem: A student dislikes the booking service a club chose and assumes the treasurer ignored cost. The treasurer has not explained the choice. How should the student proceed?

options.text: Present carelessness as the cause because the chosen service is expensive.
options.rationale: Price alone does not establish the decision-maker’s reasoning or constraints.

options.text: Seek an appropriate explanation of alternatives and constraints, and leave the reason unknown until supported.
options.rationale: Observation should distinguish the person’s account from the student’s inference.

options.text: Invent a reasonable motive so the written account has a complete story.
options.rationale: A plausible invented reason cannot teach how the decision was actually made.

options.text: Assume every decision by an officer is well reasoned and needs no examination.
options.rationale: Respectful inquiry does not require uncritical acceptance.

section: Get close to a decision
objective: Use criticism to revise work while preserving evidence of learning
stem: A junior analyst’s process comparison overlooks amended orders. A colleague points out the omission. What response best supports learning?

options.text: Remove the colleague’s comment so the original comparison appears complete.
options.rationale: That hides a gap rather than correcting it.

options.text: Discard every conclusion because one exception was missed.
options.rationale: The omission warrants a targeted reassessment, not automatic rejection of all the work.

options.text: Keep the comparison unchanged to demonstrate confidence.
options.rationale: Confidence does not address the omitted case.

options.text: Revise the comparison to examine amended orders and keep the earlier version with the correction explained.
options.rationale: The change makes both the reasoning and what improved visible.

section: Use a tool without borrowing its confidence
objective: Check the unit behind a generated complaint count
stem: A tool reports that delivery complaints doubled. Several messages may concern the same unresolved order. What should the distributor’s analyst check first?

options.text: Whether the count represents messages, customers, orders or unresolved cases.
options.rationale: Different units can give different meanings to the claimed increase.

options.text: Whether the summary uses stronger language to convey urgency.
options.rationale: Wording does not establish what was counted.

options.text: Whether every repeated message can automatically be treated as a new customer.
options.rationale: That would assume the point that needs checking.

options.text: Whether a larger message total proves a larger number of distinct failures.
options.rationale: Repeated contact may increase messages without increasing distinct cases.

section: Use a tool without borrowing its confidence
objective: Interpret counts using comparable exposure before recommending action
stem: A distributor had 20 complaint cases among 1,000 orders, then 40 among 2,000 orders, using the same definition. What is the best initial interpretation?

options.text: The complaint rate doubled because the case count doubled.
options.rationale: The order volume doubled too.

options.text: Customer service necessarily improved because the business grew.
options.rationale: The figures do not establish improvement in handling or experience.

options.text: The rate stayed at 2%, while the absolute workload rose; investigate the decision-relevant consequences before recommending a change.
options.rationale: Both the stable rate and increased number of cases matter, but they answer different questions.

options.text: The complaint count is irrelevant because the rate is unchanged.
options.rationale: Forty cases can impose more work or harm than twenty even at the same rate.

section: Use a tool without borrowing its confidence
objective: Match verification effort to the claims and consequences of submitted work
stem: A student uses a tool for a private outline and for a recommendation that commits the club’s budget. How should review differ?

options.text: Both need no checking if the language is fluent.
options.rationale: Fluency does not support the underlying claims.

options.text: Check the recommendation’s decision-critical inputs, calculations and sources more carefully because its consequences are greater.
options.rationale: Verification should fit the consequence and focus on claims that support the decision.

options.text: Every sentence in both drafts must receive identical review regardless of its role.
options.rationale: The chapter calls for proportionate review, not identical treatment of all outputs.

options.text: Only the private outline needs checking because it contains fewer words.
options.rationale: Length is not the main determinant of decision risk.

section: Use a tool without borrowing its confidence
objective: Keep a material assumption visible at handoff
stem: A tool-assisted estimate of club booking costs assumes the same number of users next year. The officer removes that qualification to make the recommendation sound cleaner. What is lost?

options.text: Only a stylistic detail with no decision relevance.
options.rationale: A different user count could change the estimate.

options.text: A guarantee that next year’s user count will remain constant.
options.rationale: The qualification never guaranteed that assumption.

options.text: The right to use any tool for the estimate.
options.rationale: The issue is support for the result, not tool use itself.

options.text: A visible condition the decision-maker needs to evaluate and revisit.
options.rationale: Hiding an assumption makes a conditional estimate appear more certain than its evidence supports.

section: Use a tool without borrowing its confidence
objective: Choose practice material consistent with confidentiality and permission
stem: A distributor intern wants to practise summarising complaints with a convenient online tool. The available examples contain confidential customer information and no approval covers that use. What is appropriate?

options.text: Use fictional or appropriately approved material and follow the organisation’s tool-use rules.
options.rationale: Convenience does not authorise disclosure of confidential records.

options.text: Upload the records because the purpose is education rather than profit.
options.rationale: A learning purpose does not remove confidentiality obligations.

options.text: Remove names and assume all remaining records are safe to disclose.
options.rationale: Other fields may still identify people or reveal confidential business information.

options.text: Upload first and ask for permission only if the output seems useful.
options.rationale: A later benefit does not supply permission for the initial disclosure.

section: Build the part that accumulates
objective: Build domain understanding by following a transaction across departments
stem: A new distributor employee knows the names of its software products but cannot explain why a corrected order affects billing. What practice would best deepen that understanding?

options.text: Memorise more vendor abbreviations before speaking with accounts.
options.rationale: Vocabulary alone will not explain the work and dependencies.

options.text: Study only the order-entry screen because other departments own the rest.
options.rationale: The correction’s consequences cross the departmental boundary.

options.text: Follow an authorised example from order through delivery and invoice, including a correction and its consequences.
options.rationale: A concrete transaction reveals records, handoffs and why other roles care about an error.

options.text: Assume every department uses the same definition because the software is shared.
options.rationale: Shared software does not establish identical interpretations or responsibilities.

section: Build the part that accumulates
objective: Demonstrate reliability by openly correcting a submitted error
stem: A club officer discovers a calculation error in a cost comparison already shared with the committee. What best demonstrates reliability?

options.text: Wait to see whether anyone notices before deciding to mention it.
options.rationale: That leaves others relying on an error the officer knows about.

options.text: Explain the error, provide the corrected calculation and state whether the recommendation changes.
options.rationale: Open correction gives colleagues a basis to reassess and trust the work.

options.text: Quietly overwrite the file without telling people who used the earlier result.
options.rationale: They may continue acting on the old figure without knowing it changed.

options.text: Blame the calculation tool and leave the recommendation unchanged without checking.
options.rationale: Tool involvement does not remove responsibility for examining the error’s consequences.

section: What this book was arguing
objective: Identify the book’s central explanation of technology outcomes
stem: Which statement best expresses the book’s central argument?

options.text: A sufficiently capable tool determines the business outcome on its own.
options.rationale: Outcomes also depend on work, records, authority and measures of success.

options.text: Technology decisions belong entirely to technical specialists.
options.rationale: Business decisions shape the arrangements the technology supports.

options.text: Asking good questions eliminates the need for technical work and adequate resources.
options.rationale: Questions must lead to evidence, competent work and follow-through.

options.text: Technology enables arrangements, while people’s decisions about work, records, authority and success shape the outcome.
options.rationale: The book treats the information system as a business arrangement rather than software alone.

section: What this book was arguing
objective: Separate useful service improvement from durable competitive advantage
stem: A distributor adopts a tool that reduces order errors, and competitors can obtain the same capability cheaply. What follows?

options.text: The improvement may create useful value without establishing an advantage the distributor can sustain over rivals.
options.rationale: Better performance and lasting differentiation are separate claims.

options.text: The improvement has no value because others can copy it.
options.rationale: Useful service can matter even when it does not create a durable edge.

options.text: Lower error rates prove the distributor now has a permanent advantage.
options.rationale: The stated ease of copying leaves that conclusion unsupported.

options.text: Using technology automatically makes the distributor more profitable than every competitor.
options.rationale: The label does not settle costs, implementation or rivals’ performance.

section: What this book was arguing
objective: Separate capability growth from an investor’s return
stem: A campus enterprise proposes investing in a digital service because the underlying capability is spreading rapidly. What remains unestablished?

options.text: Whether rapid adoption means any customer could find the capability useful.
options.rationale: Adoption can support interest in the capability, though it does not settle this investment.

options.text: Whether a widely used technology must stop growing before investment is possible.
options.rationale: There is no such prerequisite.

options.text: Who will pay this enterprise enough, for long enough, to cover its commitments and justify the investment.
options.rationale: Direction of adoption does not establish where durable economic returns will accrue.

options.text: Whether technical popularity alone can replace evidence about demand and cost.
options.rationale: It cannot; treating it as a substitute is the unsupported reasoning at issue.

section: What this book was arguing
objective: Include dependencies beyond the organisation’s direct control in a recommendation
stem: A distributor’s proposed service depends on a supplier, network access and power outside its direct control. How should these enter its recommendation?

options.text: Exclude them because another organisation operates them.
options.rationale: External ownership does not remove the distributor’s dependence.

options.text: Identify their effects on the work, the arrangements for failure and what uncertainty remains.
options.rationale: Local outcomes depend on external systems, so the business needs to understand the consequences.

options.text: Assume the service cannot be worthwhile unless every dependency is owned internally.
options.rationale: Dependence can be acceptable when understood and managed.

options.text: Mention them only after an interruption proves they matter.
options.rationale: The commitment should consider relevant dependencies before failure occurs.

section: Your turn, last time
objective: Evaluate reasoning using evidence available at the decision rather than outcome alone
stem: A distributor made a bounded investment using defensible evidence and recorded risks. An unexpected disruption later produced a loss. How should the decision be reviewed?

options.text: The loss alone proves the original reasoning was careless.
options.rationale: An adverse outcome does not by itself establish poor ex-ante judgment.

options.text: The original evidence means no later review or learning is needed.
options.rationale: Decision quality also involves responding when information changes.

options.text: Any profitable alternative must have been obvious at the time.
options.rationale: A later comparison can introduce knowledge unavailable to the original decision-maker.

options.text: Examine what was known, how risks and alternatives were handled, and the response to new information.
options.rationale: The review distinguishes decision quality from luck while preserving accountability for follow-through.

section: Your turn, last time
objective: Recognise learning that improves precision without reversing a conclusion
stem: A club officer still supports the same booking service after checking evidence, but now states the cost horizon and exception-handling limits clearly. Must the conclusion change to demonstrate learning?

options.text: No; better definitions and explicit limits can improve the reasoning while preserving the recommendation.
options.rationale: Learning can sharpen a supported claim without requiring a different verdict.

options.text: Yes; keeping the conclusion proves the review added nothing.
options.rationale: Precision and evidential support can improve even when the preferred choice stays the same.

options.text: No; the unchanged conclusion means the original vague explanation was sufficient.
options.rationale: The more precise explanation addresses gaps in the original reasoning.

options.text: Yes; every review should alternate the preferred choice to avoid bias.
options.rationale: A changed answer is not a substitute for evidence-based judgment.
